name: Kasongo Luunda
description: Kasongo Luunda emerged as an autonomous kingdom of the Yaka people in the Kwango River basin during the early eighteenth century. Established through migration waves linked to the broader Lunda expansion, the realm maintained a centralised court that commanded fertile river valleys and engaged in regional caravan commerce. It preserved sovereign territorial authority until the late nineteenth century, when European partition treaties assigned the region to the Congo Free State. \n\n Status: Traditional kingdom; Capital: Kasongo Lunda; Common languages: Kiyaka, Kikongo and Lingala; Religion: Traditional African religion; Government: Absolute monarchy; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1701; Disestablished: 1 November 1885; Succeeded by: Congo Free State

name: Kiang
description: Kiang was a sovereign Mandinka riverine kingdom situated along the southern banks of the lower Gambia River. The state commanded vital fluvial trade routes linking inland agricultural settlements with Atlantic coastal merchants, exchanging groundnuts, beeswax and grain. It retained internal independence through recurring nineteenth-century Marabout wars before British colonial forces absorbed its districts into the Gambia Protectorate in 1901. \n\n Status: Riverine kingdom; Capital: Kiang; Common languages: Mandinka; Religion: Traditional African religion and Islam; Government: Monarchy; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1701; Disestablished: 1901; Succeeded by: British Gambia

name: Kingdom of Gourma
description: The Kingdom of Gourma, also known historically as Gulmu, was an autonomous West African state founded by the Gurma people across the savannahs of eastern Burkina Faso. Governed from its capital at Fada N'Gourma by a hereditary paramount ruler styled the Nunbado, the realm preserved a sophisticated cavalry force and defended its borders against Mossi neighbours. Its independence endured until French colonial military columns annexed the territory at the turn of the twentieth century. \n\n Status: Traditional kingdom; Capital: Fada N'Gourma; Common languages: Gourmanchéma; Religion: Traditional African religion; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Ruler title: Nunbado; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1701; Disestablished: 1900; Succeeded by: French West Africa

name: Kingdom of Igala
description: The Kingdom of Igala flourished as a major riverine empire centred on its royal bluff citadel at Idah near the Niger-Benue confluence in modern-day central Nigeria. Governed by a divine monarch styled the Ata, the kingdom maintained a formidable fleet of war canoes that dominated inland navigation and regulated commercial traffic throughout the lower Niger basin. The realm retained full political independence until British imperial forces subjugated the monarchical apparatus in 1902. \n\n Status: Traditional kingdom; Capital: Idah; Common languages: Igala; Religion: Ojo (traditional faith); Government: Sacred monarchy; Ruler title: Ata; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1701; Disestablished: 1902; Succeeded by: Northern Nigeria Protectorate

name: Kingdom of Igala
description: The Kingdom of Igala exercised extensive sovereign hegemony across the middle belt savannahs of the lower Niger Valley throughout the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. Supported by elaborate state rituals, ironworking industries and dynastic ties with neighbouring Idoma and Nupe communities, the Ata governed through a council of royal elders based at Idah. Imperial British campaigns formally incorporated the historic kingdom into the Protectorate of Northern Nigeria at the start of the twentieth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Idah; Common languages: Igala; Religion: Ojo (traditional faith); Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruler title: Ata; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1701; Disestablished: 1902; Succeeded by: British Empire

name: Kingdom of Mangareva
description: The Kingdom of Mangareva was an autonomous Polynesian island monarchy that encompassed the volcanic peaks and coral lagoons of the Gambier archipelago in the south-eastern Pacific Ocean. Ruled from the royal village of Rikitea by high chiefs drawn from the noble togoiti class and styled the akariki, the kingdom sustained a maritime economy founded on lagoon fishing and agriculture. Indigenous rule persisted until January 1844, when the monarchical council accepted French protectorate status following Catholic missionary influence. \n\n Status: Island monarchy; Capital: Rikitea; Common languages: Mangarevan; Religion: Traditional Polynesian religion; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Ruler title: Akariki; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1701; Reorganised: 16 January 1844; Succeeded by: French Protectorate of Mangareva

name: Kingdom of Nembe
description: The Kingdom of Nembe was an influential Ijaw trading realm situated amidst the labyrinthine waterways and mangrove swamps of the central Niger Delta. The monarchy derived immense strategic wealth by brokering commercial exchanges between hinterland oil palm producers and visiting European ocean-going vessels. Governed by an Amanyanabo from the royal capital of Nembe, the state preserved sovereign maritime authority until British authorities established the Oil Rivers Protectorate in June 1885. \n\n Status: Delta kingdom; Capital: Nembe; Common languages: Ijaw (Nembe); Religion: Traditional African religion; Government: Elective monarchy; Ruler title: Amanyanabo; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1701; Disestablished: 5 June 1885; Succeeded by: Oil Rivers Protectorate

name: Kingdom of Niue
description: The Kingdom of Niue arose on an isolated raised coral atoll in western Polynesia when disparate local districts unified under a single monarchical institution. Governed by an elected king styled the Patu-iki who presided from Alofi, the realm balanced communal island councils with central sacred rituals. This sovereign Polynesian polity maintained independent domestic authority until late nineteenth-century diplomatic petitions led to the proclamation of a British protectorate in 1898. \n\n Status: Island monarchy; Capital: Alofi; Common languages: Niuean; Religion: Traditional Polynesian religion; Government: Elective monarchy; Ruler title: Patu-iki; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1701; Disestablished: 30 June 1898; Succeeded by: British Protectorate of Niue

name: Kingdom of Orungu
description: The Kingdom of Orungu was an autonomous maritime thalassocracy established by Myene-speaking clans around Cape Lopez and the lower Ogooue River delta on the Atlantic coast of central Africa. Ruled by a sovereign monarch styled the Agamwinboni, the kingdom monopolised riverine commerce and became a pre-eminent Atlantic trading hub for timber, ivory and regional commodities. Political centralisation remained robust until naval shifts and French commercial expansion eclipsed the monarchy during the 1870s. \n\n Status: Coastal thalassocracy; Capital: Port-Gentil; Common languages: Orungu (Myene); Religion: Traditional African religion; Government: Elective monarchy; Ruler title: Agamwinboni; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1701; Disestablished: 1874; Succeeded by: French Gabon

name: Kingogo
description: Kingogo was an autonomous precolonial highland kingdom located in the rugged mountainous country of north-western Rwanda. The realm functioned under hereditary dynastic lineages who defended local grazing pastures, managed agricultural terracing and preserved distinct ritual customs independent of the centralising Nyiginya court. It resisted royal annexation for generations before early twentieth-century Belgian colonial consolidation integrated the chieftaincy into the wider Rwandan administrative system. \n\n Status: Traditional highland kingdom; Capital: Kingogo; Common languages: Kinyarwanda; Religion: Traditional African religion; Government: Hereditary chieftaincy; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1701; Disestablished: 1926; Succeeded by: Ruanda-Urundi

name: Kokoro
description: Kokoro was an autonomous Sahelian principality situated in the dry plains of western Niger near the modern border with Burkina Faso. Operating as a fortified garrison settlement and commercial centre, the state maintained armed cavalry to protect caravan junctions and surrounding agrarian communities against nomadic raiders. Sovereign governance endured until the French military advance at the turn of the twentieth century brought the territory under colonial rule. \n\n Status: Sahelian principality; Capital: Kokoro; Common languages: Songhai and Fulfulde; Religion: Islam and Traditional African religion; Government: Traditional monarchy; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1701; Disestablished: 1900; Succeeded by: French West Africa

name: Lesser Kyamutwara
label: african great lakes kingdoms
description: Lesser Kyamutwara was an autonomous Haya kingdom situated along the western shores of Lake Victoria around modern-day Bukoba in north-western Tanzania. Following the historic partition of the greater Kyamutwara domain, the state was ruled by a hereditary monarch styled the Mukama who oversaw fertile banana groves, cattle husbandry and iron smelting. The principality retained sovereignty until German East Africa forces established colonial administrative posts across the lake region in 1891. \n\n Status: Great Lakes kingdom; Capital: Bukoba; Common languages: Haya; Religion: Traditional African religion; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Ruler title: Mukama; Historical era: Early modern period; Historical region: African Great Lakes; Established: 1701; Disestablished: 1891; Succeeded by: German East Africa

name: Luba Empire
description: The Luba Empire was a highly organised Central African kingdom centred in the marshy lake systems and savannas of the Upemba Depression in south-eastern Congo. Governed from royal capitals such as Mwibele by a divine ruler styled the mulopwe, the empire commanded regional trade in copper, salt and dried fish through an elite society of ritual titleholders known as the Bambudye. Internal succession disputes and armed incursions by foreign slave raiders weakened the state prior to its subjugation by the Congo Free State in 1890. \n\n Status: Imperial monarchy; Capital: Mwibele; Common languages: Kiluba; Religion: Traditional Luba religion; Government: Sacred monarchy; Ruler title: Mulopwe; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1701; Disestablished: 1890; Succeeded by: Congo Free State

name: Machame
label: african great lakes kingdoms
description: Machame was a powerful Chagga kingdom situated on the forested south-western slopes of Mount Kilimanjaro in north-eastern Tanzania. Formidable agricultural terracing, deep defensive trenches and an effective warrior hierarchy enabled the monarch, styled the Mangi, to forge a dominant confederation over neighbouring mountain polities. The kingdom retained its sovereign independence until the Imperial German East Africa Company and German military forces imposed colonial vassalage in 1891. \n\n Status: Mountain kingdom; Capital: Machame; Common languages: Kichagga; Religion: Traditional Chagga religion; Government: Chieftaincy; Ruler title: Mangi; Historical era: Early modern period; Historical region: African Great Lakes; Established: 1701; Disestablished: 1891; Succeeded by: German East Africa

name: Maw State
label: shan states
description: Maw State was an autonomous Shan principality situated in the Myelat region along the western slopes of the Shan Hills within the Zawgyi River basin. Ruled by a hereditary chief bearing the title Ngwegunhmu, the state governed a predominantly Danu and Shan population engaged in valley agriculture and highland mineral trade. While paying tribute to the Burmese Konbaung monarchy, Maw retained extensive domestic autonomy until British imperial forces annexed the Shan plateau in 1886. \n\n Status: Tributary princely state; Capital: Maw; Common languages: Danu, Shan and Burmese; Religion: Theravada Buddhism; Government: Feudal principality; Ruler title: Ngwegunhmu; Historical era: Early modern period; Historical region: Shan States; Established: 1701; Disestablished: 1886; Succeeded by: British Burma

name: Mbailundu
description: Mbailundu, often recorded as Bailundo, was one of the largest and most powerful Ovimbundu kingdoms on the central plateau of modern-day Angola. Led by a paramount monarch styled the Soma Inene who reigned from the fortified mountain redoubt of Halavala near Bailundo, the realm commanded long-distance trade caravans connecting inland regions with Atlantic ports. The kingdom fiercely defended its autonomy against Portuguese colonial expansion until being conquered following the Bailundo War of 1902 to 1904. \n\n Status: Highland kingdom; Capital: Bailundo; Common languages: Umbundu; Religion: Traditional African religion; Government: Elective monarchy; Ruler title: Soma Inene; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1701; Disestablished: 1904; Succeeded by: Portuguese West Africa

name: Monghsat State
label: shan states
description: Monghsat State was an inland Shan principality located in the rugged highlands of the southern Shan States near the border with modern Thailand. Governed by a hereditary Saopha, the realm maintained agrarian valleys and protected highland caravan tracks connecting the Salween and Mekong basins. Although bound by vassalage and annual tribute to the Burmese court, the principality managed its internal administration independently until British colonial authorities annexed the region in 1886. \n\n Status: Tributary princely state; Capital: Mong Hsat; Common languages: Shan and Burmese; Religion: Theravada Buddhism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruler title: Saopha; Historical era: Early modern period; Historical region: Shan States; Established: 1701; Disestablished: 1886; Succeeded by: British Burma

name: Mutondo
description: Mutondo was an autonomous precolonial kingdom established by the Nkoya people across the woodland savannahs of what is now Kaoma District in western Zambia. The realm was ruled by a royal lineage headed by the Mwene Mutondo, who maintained elaborate ancestral courts, royal drum ensembles and sacred regalia. Sovereign control over local ivory and forest resources continued until late nineteenth-century Lozi expansion and the British South Africa Company established administrative hegemony in 1891. \n\n Status: Traditional kingdom; Capital: Mutondo; Common languages: Nkoya; Religion: Traditional African religion; Government: Sacred monarchy; Ruler title: Mwene Mutondo; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1701; Disestablished: 1891; Succeeded by: British South Africa Company

name: Niamina
description: Niamina was a sovereign Mandinka kingdom situated along the central reaches of the Gambia River in West Africa. The realm exercised control over riverine shipping and fertile alluvial plains, providing agricultural commodities and river pilotage to regional merchants. It preserved its local dynastic governance through nineteenth-century Soninke-Marabout conflicts before British colonial forces absorbed its districts into the Gambia Protectorate in 1901. \n\n Status: Riverine kingdom; Capital: Niamina; Common languages: Mandinka; Religion: Traditional African religion and Islam; Government: Chieftaincy; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1701; Disestablished: 1901; Succeeded by: British Gambia

name: Nyamwanga
label: african great lakes kingdoms
description: Nyamwanga was an autonomous Bantu kingdom established by the Namwanga people across the fertile plateau spanning modern north-eastern Zambia and south-western Tanzania. Centred around Nakonde, the realm was led by a traditional sovereign styled the Mukoma who coordinated agricultural production, cattle raising and cross-plateau trade networks. The kingdom preserved independent authority until Anglo-German colonial boundary demarcation partitioned the region between British Northern Rhodesia and German East Africa in 1891. \n\n Status: Traditional kingdom; Capital: Nakonde; Common languages: Namwanga; Religion: Traditional African religion; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Ruler title: Mukoma; Historical era: Early modern period; Historical region: African Great Lakes; Established: 1701; Disestablished: 1891; Succeeded by: British South Africa Company

name: Okpoama
description: Okpoama was an autonomous coastal city-state established by the Ijaw people on the Atlantic shoreline of the Niger Delta in southern Nigeria. Functioning as an independent branch of the broader Brass and Nembe cultural zone, the community was governed by an Amanyanabo who regulated canoe trade, salt production and commercial transactions with European vessels. Sovereign autonomy ended in 1891 when the British government consolidated the region under the Oil Rivers Protectorate. \n\n Status: Coastal city-state; Capital: Okpoama; Common languages: Ijaw (Nembe); Religion: Traditional African religion; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Amanyanabo; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1701; Disestablished: 1891; Succeeded by: Oil Rivers Protectorate

name: Paraku
description: Paraku was an autonomous Bariba trading principality situated in the interior savannah of northern Benin. Serving as an important crossroads for trans-Saharan caravans travelling between the Hausa kingdoms and the Guinea coast, the city-kingdom grew wealthy through the regulation of livestock, kola nut and textile markets. Local Bariba rulers governed the settlement until French military forces captured the town during the Dahomey and Borgu campaigns in 1895. \n\n Status: Traditional principality; Capital: Parakou; Common languages: Bariba; Religion: Traditional African religion and Islam; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1701; Disestablished: 1895; Succeeded by: French Dahomey

name: Shavasha
description: Shavasha was a precolonial Shona kingdom situated on the highveld plateau of north-eastern Zimbabwe near modern-day Harare. Established by the Vashawasha people under their dynastic rulers, the state developed extensive agricultural villages, cattle pasturage and regional trading links with neighbouring Karanga polities. The kingdom retained its sovereignty until the arrival of the British South Africa Company Pioneer Column and subsequent colonial settlement in 1890. \n\n Status: Traditional kingdom; Capital: Chishawasha; Common languages: Shona; Religion: Traditional African religion; Government: Hereditary chieftaincy; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1701; Disestablished: 1890; Succeeded by: British South Africa Company

name: Sultanate of Logone-Birni
description: The Sultanate of Logone-Birni was a prominent Kotoko riverine state situated along the western banks of the Logone River south of Lake Chad in northern Cameroon. Governed from a heavily fortified earthen capital by a monarch styled the Miarre, the principality commanded important fishing waters, river ferry crossings and regional trade routes. It maintained independent diplomatic and military standing until the Fulani jihad launched from Sokoto overran its northern defences in 1806. \n\n Status: Traditional sultanate; Capital: Logone-Birni; Common languages: Kotoko and Kanuri; Religion: Islam; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Miarre; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1701; Disestablished: 1806; Succeeded by: Bornu Empire

name: Sultanate of Tadjoura
description: The Sultanate of Tadjoura was an influential maritime Afar realm established along the northern shoreline of the Gulf of Tadjoura in the Horn of Africa. Ruled by a traditional sovereign styled the Dardar, the port served as the primary coastal gateway for lucrative caravan trails transporting coffee, salt, slaves and hides from the Ethiopian interior. Sovereign authority persisted until June 1884, when the reigning sultan concluded a treaty ceding territorial protection to France. \n\n Status: Coastal sultanate; Capital: Tadjoura; Common languages: Afar and Arabic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Traditional monarchy; Ruler title: Dardar; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1701; Disestablished: 24 June 1884; Succeeded by: French Somaliland

name: Tera
description: Tera was an autonomous Sahelian principality located in the Tillaberi basin of western Niger near the modern border with Burkina Faso. Inhabited primarily by Songhai and Gourmantche communities, the realm defended vital agricultural plains and riverine tracks against nomadic Touareg raiders. The local dynasty exercised self-rule until expanding French colonial expeditions incorporated the territory into the Military Territory of Niger in 1900. \n\n Status: Sahelian principality; Capital: Téra; Common languages: Songhai and Gourmanchéma; Religion: Islam and Traditional African religion; Government: Traditional chieftaincy; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1701; Disestablished: 1900; Succeeded by: French West Africa

name: Tomani
description: Tomani was a historic Mandinka kingdom situated along the south bank of the upper Gambia River in West Africa. Centred at the historic commercial hub of Sutuko, the realm commanded extensive agricultural territory and prospered by regulating riverine shipping and overland trade connecting Senegambia with the interior. The kingdom maintained sovereign institutions through decades of regional religious wars until the British administration absorbed the area into the Gambia Protectorate in 1901. \n\n Status: Riverine kingdom; Capital: Sutuko; Common languages: Mandinka; Religion: Traditional African religion and Islam; Government: Monarchy; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1701; Disestablished: 1901; Succeeded by: British Gambia

name: Ufipa
label: african great lakes kingdoms
description: Ufipa was an autonomous Great Lakes kingdom located across the fertile Ufipa Plateau between Lake Tanganyika and Lake Rukwa in south-western Tanzania. Governed by the Milanzi and later the Tembwe dynasties of the Fipa people, the state was renowned for sophisticated ironworking, terraced cultivation and complex ritual court structures. The realm maintained independent political authority until German imperial colonial troops occupied the plateau in 1891. \n\n Status: Great Lakes kingdom; Capital: Sumbawanga; Common languages: Fipa; Religion: Traditional African religion; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Mwene; Historical era: Early modern period; Historical region: African Great Lakes; Established: 1701; Disestablished: 1891; Succeeded by: German East Africa

name: Ugweno
label: african great lakes kingdoms
description: Ugweno was a centralised highland kingdom situated in the northern Pare Mountains of north-eastern Tanzania. Established under the Suya dynasty, the realm developed an elaborate administrative bureaucracy, an organised military network and extensive mountain irrigation systems to support its terraced agriculture. The kingdom retained sovereign independence from coastal and inland powers until the German imperial administration brought the Pare region under colonial rule in 1891. \n\n Status: Highland kingdom; Capital: Ugweno; Common languages: Kigweno; Religion: Traditional African religion; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Ruler title: Mangi; Historical era: Early modern period; Historical region: African Great Lakes; Established: 1701; Disestablished: 1891; Succeeded by: German East Africa

name: Uukwambi
description: Uukwambi was an autonomous precolonial kingdom of the Ovambo people situated across the flat plains of northern Namibia. Ruled by a hereditary monarch styled the omukwaniilwa from the royal centre at Elim, the kingdom operated complex agricultural systems, raised cattle and maintained skilled metalworking guilds. Sovereign governance was fiercely defended against external encroachment until the German Empire gradually extended colonial protection over the Ovambo kingdoms in 1896. \n\n Status: Traditional kingdom; Capital: Elim; Common languages: Oshikwambi; Religion: Traditional African religion; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Ruler title: Omukwaniilwa; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1701; Disestablished: 1896; Succeeded by: German South West Africa

name: Prussian Gold Coast
description: The Prussian Gold Coast comprised a network of fortified commercial settlements along the Gulf of Guinea centred on Fort Gross Friedrichsburg at modern-day Princes Town. Originally founded by the Margraviate of Brandenburg in 1682, the colony was transferred to Prussian royal administration following the coronation of Frederick I in January 1701. The enterprise struggled with supply constraints and native resistance before King Frederick William I formally sold the coastal outposts to the Dutch West India Company in 1721. \n\n Status: Overseas colony; Capital: Princes Town; Common languages: German and Akan; Religion: Protestantism; Government: Colonial governorship; Head of state: Frederick I; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 15 January 1701; Disestablished: 1722; Preceded by: Brandenburger Gold Coast; Succeeded by: Dutch Gold Coast

name: Kingdom of Prussia
description: The Kingdom of Prussia encompassed the Hohenzollern monarchical domains situated outside the legal borders of the Holy Roman Empire, centred historically on Ducal Prussia and the coronation city of Königsberg. Because sovereign titles within the Empire were restricted, Elector Frederick III crowned himself King in Prussia in January 1701, transforming this eastern Baltic possession into a sovereign kingdom. The territory served as the legal and ideological foundation for Hohenzollern great-power status until the dissolution of the Holy Roman Empire in 1806. \n\n Status: Royal possession; Capital: Königsberg; Common languages: German, Polish and Lithuanian; Religion: Lutheranism and Calvinism; Government: Absolute monarchy; Ruler title: King in Prussia; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 18 January 1701; Disestablished: 6 August 1806; Preceded by: Duchy of Prussia; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Prussia (unified)

name: Kingdom of Prussia
label: holy roman empire;german confederation
description: The Kingdom of Prussia was a major Central European great power ruled by the House of Hohenzollern with its seat of government at Berlin. Arising from the union of the Margraviate of Brandenburg with eastern ducal lands, the kingdom developed a famously disciplined army, an efficient civil bureaucracy and vast industrial capacity. Prussia steered northern German political affairs through the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, ultimately culminating in the proclamation of the unified German Empire in January 1871. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Berlin; Common languages: German; Religion: Protestantism (Lutheran and Calvinist); Government: Semi-constitutional monarchy; Ruler title: King of Prussia; Legislature: Landtag; Historical era: Modern era; Established: 18 January 1701; Disestablished: 18 January 1871; Succeeded by: German Empire

name: Ashanti Empire
label: akan states
description: The Ashanti Empire was a powerful Akan state that dominated the forested interior and coastal trade routes of modern-day Ghana. Unified under King Osei Tutu and the high priest Okomfo Anokye around the spiritual emblem of the Golden Stool, the empire established a sophisticated military and administrative system based at Kumasi. The realm grew exceptionally wealthy through the export of gold, kola nuts and slaves, resisting British military incursions until being subjected to imperial occupation in 1896. \n\n Status: Imperial monarchy; Capital: Kumasi; Common languages: Asante Twi; Religion: Akan religion; Government: Elective confederate monarchy; Ruler title: Asantehene; Historical era: Early modern period; Historical region: Akan States; Established: 1702; Disestablished: 1896; Succeeded by: British Gold Coast

name: Duchy of Mecklenburg-Strelitz
label: holy roman empire;confederation of the rhine
description: The Duchy of Mecklenburg-Strelitz was an imperial state of the Holy Roman Empire established in north-eastern Germany following the dynastic partition of the House of Mecklenburg in 1701. Ruled from Neustrelitz, the principality comprised the historic Lordship of Stargard in eastern Mecklenburg along with the western exclave of the Principality of Ratzeburg. It navigated the Napoleonic Wars within the Confederation of the Rhine before being elevated to a grand duchy at the Congress of Vienna in 1815. \n\n Status: Imperial duchy; Capital: Neustrelitz; Common languages: German and Low German; Religion: Lutheranism; Government: Duchy; Ruler title: Duke of Mecklenburg-Strelitz; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1702; Disestablished: 28 June 1815; Preceded by: Duchy of Mecklenburg; Succeeded by: Grand Duchy of Mecklenburg-Strelitz

name: Kalhora Dynasty
description: The Kalhora Dynasty governed Sindh as a semi-autonomous principality within the declining Mughal Empire during the early eighteenth century. Established under Mian Yar Muhammad Kalhoro, who received imperial titles and consolidated his authority from the new capital at Khudabad, the state constructed extensive irrigation canals and fostered regional commerce. The dynasty exercised effective local sovereignty until Persian forces under Nader Shah invaded the Indus Valley in 1739 and imposed tributary subjection. \n\n Status: Semi-autonomous principality; Capital: Khudabad; Official languages: Sindhi and Persian; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Hereditary nawabship; Ruler title: Nawab (Mian); Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1702; Reorganised: 1739; Preceded by: Thatta Subah; Succeeded by: Afsharid tributary Sindh

name: Sitamau State
description: Sitamau State was an autonomous Rajput princely realm founded in 1701 by Keshav Das, a grandson of Ratan Singh of Ratlam, within the Malwa region of central India. Governing from the hilltop town of Sitamau, the Rathore rulers retained independent authority amidst the decline of imperial Mughal power and frequent Maratha raids. The principality preserved its local ruling dynasty and customary institutions throughout the eighteenth century before concluding tributary arrangements in the early nineteenth century. \n\n Status: Princely state; Capital: Sitamau; Common languages: Malvi and Hindi; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Princely monarchy; Ruler title: Raja; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1702; Disestablished: 1802; Succeeded by: Sitamau (Maratha tributary)

name: Republic of the Seven United Netherlands and Great Britain (Military Occupation)
description: The joint military occupation administered by the Republic of the Seven United Netherlands and Great Britain encompassed strategic strongpoints and river crossings in the Low Countries during the War of the Spanish Succession. Operating under the command of the Duke of Marlborough and Dutch field deputies, the allied forces secured garrisons across Upper Guelders, the Meuse valley and adjacent territories. This operational condominium managed local defence and logistics until the Treaties of Utrecht and Rastatt restored civil administration. \n\n Status: Joint military occupation; Capital: None (decentralised); Common languages: Dutch, English and German; Religion: Protestantism and Roman Catholicism; Government: Allied military administration; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1 July 1702; Disestablished: 7 September 1714; Succeeded by: Austrian Netherlands

name: Grand Alliance (Military Occupation)
description: The Grand Alliance military occupation was an emergency Austrian-led coalition administration established to oversee captured fortresses and occupied territories along the Rhine and across the southern Low Countries during the War of the Spanish Succession. Created to counter Bourbon expansionism and assert Habsburg claims to the Spanish inheritance, imperial commanders coordinated garrison logistics, revenue collection and regional defence. The provisional military regime dissolved upon the ratification of the Treaties of Rastatt and Baden in 1714. \n\n Status: Coalition military occupation; Capital: None (decentralised); Common languages: German, Latin, French and Dutch; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Military command; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 15 May 1703; Disestablished: 7 September 1714; Preceded by: Spanish Netherlands; Succeeded by: Austrian Netherlands

name: Jath State
description: Jath State was an autonomous Maratha principality established on the Deccan plateau in present-day southern Maharashtra. Founded by hereditary chiefs of the Daphle clan who held the patilship of Daphlapur, the estate exercised de facto sovereignty amidst the fracturing of the Bijapur Sultanate and the rise of the Maratha Empire. The rulers maintained local garrisons and collected regional revenues autonomously until formal subsidiary treaties were concluded in the early nineteenth century. \n\n Status: Princely state; Capital: Jath; Common languages: Marathi; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Jagir principality; Ruler title: Raja; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1705; Disestablished: 1801; Preceded by: Maratha Empire; Succeeded by: Jath (British protectorate)

name: Principality of Mindelheim
label: holy roman empire
description: The Principality of Mindelheim was an immediate imperial territory of the Holy Roman Empire created in 1705 by Emperor Joseph I for John Churchill, 1st Duke of Marlborough. Bestowed in recognition of Marlborough's decisive victory at the Battle of Blenheim during the War of the Spanish Succession, the small Swabian principality gave the British commander sovereign prince status and a seat in the Imperial Diet. The territory reverted to the Electorate of Bavaria following the peace settlements of 1714 and 1715. \n\n Status: Imperial principality; Capital: Mindelheim; Common languages: German; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Principality; Head of state: John Churchill; Ruler title: Prince of Mindelheim; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1705; Disestablished: 1715; Succeeded by: Electorate of Bavaria

name: Electorate of Hanover
label: holy roman empire
description: The Electorate of Hanover, formally known as the Electorate of Brunswick-Lüneburg, was an autonomous imperial state in north-western Germany ruled by the House of Welf. Elevated to electoral dignity in 1692, the state unified the ancestral lands of Calenberg and Celle in August 1705 under Elector George Louis. Operating as a sovereign German principality, Hanover expanded its administrative infrastructure and diplomatic influence until George Louis ascended the British throne as King George I in August 1714. \n\n Status: Electorate of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Hannover; Common languages: German and Low German; Religion: Lutheranism; Government: Principality; Ruler title: Prince-elector; Head of state: George I Louis; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 28 August 1705; Reorganised: 1 August 1714; Succeeded by: Electorate of Hanover (personal union)

name: Principality of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel
label: holy roman empire
description: The Principality of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel was an autonomous imperial state of the Holy Roman Empire situated in Lower Saxony. Separated politically from the senior Brunswick-Lüneburg line when neighbouring Hanover pursued dynastic union with Britain, the principality was ruled by a cadet branch of the House of Welf from Wolfenbüttel and later Braunschweig. It maintained an active cultural court, promoted Enlightenment sciences and supported an independent army until being incorporated into the Napoleonic Kingdom of Westphalia in 1808. \n\n Status: Imperial principality; Capital: Braunschweig; Common languages: German and Low German; Religion: Lutheranism; Government: Principality; Ruler title: Duke of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 28 August 1705; Disestablished: 1808; Preceded by: Duchy of Brunswick-Lüneburg; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Westphalia

name: Confederated Estates of the Kingdom of Hungary
description: The Confederated Estates of the Kingdom of Hungary formed an insurgent aristocratic confederation during Rakoczi War of Independence against Habsburg imperial rule. Convened at the Diet of Szechenyi under the leadership of Prince Francis II Rakoczi, the noble estates renounced Austrian suzerainty, instituted a national treasury and fielded Kuruc armed forces. name: Île Dauphine
description: Île Dauphine was the French colonial designation for the equatorial South Atlantic archipelago of Fernando de Noronha, situated off the north-eastern coast of Brazil. Occupied by French naval detachments in 1706 as a strategic maritime supply station, the islands were briefly fortified to support French shipping routes between the Atlantic and Indian oceans. After three decades of intermittent French occupation, Portuguese colonial forces from Pernambuco reoccupied the archipelago in 1738. \n\n Status: Overseas colony; Capital: Fort Dauphin; Common languages: French; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Colonial military post; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1706; Disestablished: 1738; Preceded by: Fernando de Noronha; Succeeded by: Portuguese Brazil

name: Kel Ahaggar
