description: Kel Ahaggar was a powerful pastoral Tuareg tribal confederation centred across the rugged volcanic massif of the Hoggar Mountains in the central Sahara. Governed by a supreme paramount leader styled the Amenokal, the confederacy commanded crucial trans-Saharan caravan routes, levying transit duties and exchanging livestock, salt and dates. The confederation defended its desert sovereignty against regional powers until being subjugated by French colonial military columns in 1904. \n\n Status: Tribal confederation; Capital: Tamanrasset; Common languages: Tamahaq; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Elective pastoral confederacy; Ruler title: Amenokal; Historical era: Early modern period; Historical region: Tuareg Polities; Established: 1706; Disestablished: 1904; Succeeded by: French Algeria

name: Kingdom of Great Britain
description: The Kingdom of Great Britain was established on 1 May 1707 through the Acts of Union that politically merged the Kingdom of England and the Kingdom of Scotland into a unified realm. Governed by a single parliament assembled at Westminster under a constitutional monarchy, the state established global trade dominance and built an extensive maritime empire across North America and India. The kingdom existed until the Acts of Union 1800 incorporated the Kingdom of Ireland to create the United Kingdom. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: London; Official languages: English; Religion: Protestantism (Anglicanism and Presbyterianism); Government: Constitutional monarchy; Ruler title: Monarch; Legislature: Parliament of Great Britain; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1 May 1707; Disestablished: 1801; Preceded by: Kingdom of England and Kingdom of Scotland; Succeeded by: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland

name: Bhopal State
description: Bhopal State emerged as an independent Islamic principality in the Malwa region of central India during the disintegration of imperial Mughal authority following the death of Aurangzeb. Established by the Afghan mercenary soldier Dost Mohammad Khan, the realm expanded by absorbing local Rajput fortresses and constructing fortified palaces at Islamnagar and Bhopal. The principality exercised full territorial sovereignty during its initial decades before submitting to the suzerainty of the Nizam of Hyderabad in 1724. \n\n Status: Princely state; Capital: Bhopal; Common languages: Hindustani and Persian; Religion: Islam and Hinduism; Government: Princely monarchy; Ruler title: Nawab; Head of state: Dost Mohammad Khan; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1708; Reorganised: 1724; Succeeded by: Bhopal (Hyderabad tributary)

name: Kingdom of Galam
description: The Kingdom of Galam, historically known as Gajaaga, was an autonomous Soninke kingdom situated along the upper Senegal River valley across the borderlands of modern Senegal and Mali. Ruled by the long-standing Bathily dynasty under a monarch bearing the title Tunka, the realm controlled lucrative alluvial goldfields, ivory networks and riverine commerce with Atlantic trading companies. The kingdom preserved its sovereign autonomy against neighbouring Fula realms until nineteenth-century French colonial interventions fragmented its territory. \n\n Status: Riverine kingdom; Capital: Tuabou; Common languages: Soninke; Religion: Traditional African religion and Islam; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Ruler title: Tunka; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1708; Disestablished: 1831; Succeeded by: French Senegal

name: Kingdom of Luang Phrabang
description: The Kingdom of Luang Phrabang was established in northern Laos in 1707 following the dynastic splintering of the historic Lan Xang Empire. Ruled by King Kitsarat from the revered royal seat on the upper Mekong River, the Theravada Buddhist state exercised independent authority over northern mountain valleys and neighbouring tributary chieftains. The realm maintained complete sovereignty until expanding Burmese armies invaded the region and forced the monarchy into tributary vassalage in 1766. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Luang Phrabang; Common languages: Lao; Religion: Theravada Buddhism; Government: Absolute monarchy; Ruler title: King; Head of state: Kitsarat; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1708; Reorganised: 1766; Preceded by: Lan Xang; Succeeded by: Luang Phrabang (Burmese vassal)

name: Kingdom of Vientiane
description: The Kingdom of Vientiane emerged as a sovereign Lao successor state in 1707 in the wake of the territorial partition of the Lan Xang monarchy. Governed by King Setthathirath II from the capital city of Vientiane on the Mekong River, the realm exercised political hegemony over the fertile central plains and cultivated tributary ties with neighbouring kingdoms. The state functioned as an independent monarchy until Burmese military expeditions subordinated the realm to tributary status in 1766. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Vientiane; Common languages: Lao; Religion: Theravada Buddhism; Government: Absolute monarchy; Ruler title: King; Head of state: Setthathirath II; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1708; Reorganised: 1766; Preceded by: Lan Xang; Succeeded by: Vientiane (Burmese vassal)

name: Kolhapur State
description: Kolhapur State was an autonomous Maratha kingdom established in the Western Ghats of southern Maharashtra following a dynastic split within the House of Shivaji. Led by Maharani Tarabai and her son Shivaji II, the Bhonsle branch at Kolhapur established an independent court that rivalled the Peshwa administration at Satara. The state maintained sovereign military forces and pursued regional maritime commerce until concluding subsidiary alliance treaties with the British East India Company in 1812 and 1813. \n\n Status: Princely state; Capital: Kolhapur; Common languages: Marathi; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Princely monarchy; Ruler title: Raja; Ruling dynasty: Bhonsle; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1708; Disestablished: 1813; Preceded by: Maratha Empire; Succeeded by: Kolhapur (British protectorate)

name: Patiala State
description: Patiala State was an autonomous Sikh kingdom established across the eastern Punjab plains by Sardar Ala Singh of the Phulkian Sidhu Jat clan. Following the decline of Mughal authority, the dynasty expanded its fortified settlements, founded the capital city of Patiala and resisted repeated invasions from the Afghan Durrani Empire. The kingdom governed its fertile agrarian territories with sovereign autonomy until entering the British sphere of influence during the Second Anglo-Maratha War in 1803. \n\n Status: Princely kingdom; Capital: Patiala; Common languages: Punjabi; Religion: Sikhism, Hinduism and Islam; Government: Princely monarchy; Ruler title: Maharaja; Head of state: Ala Singh; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1708; Disestablished: 1802; Succeeded by: Patiala (British protectorate)

name: Principality of Hà Tiên
description: The Principality of Hà Tiên was an autonomous coastal domain established at the mouth of the Giang Thanh River on the Gulf of Thailand by Chinese merchant Mạc Cửu. Positioned strategically along maritime trade routes between Siam, Cambodia and Vietnam, the principality flourished as an international trading entrepot while accepting the protectorate suzerainty of the Vietnamese Nguyen lords. The autonomous principality was formally dissolved and integrated as a direct province of Vietnam by Emperor Minh Mang in 1832. \n\n Status: Autonomous protectorate; Capital: Hà Tiên; Common languages: Vietnamese, Cantonese and Khmer; Religion: Mahayana Buddhism and Confucianism; Government: Principality; Ruler title: Governor (Trấn thủ); Ruling dynasty: Mạc; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1708; Disestablished: 1833; Succeeded by: Vietnam (Nguyễn dynasty)

name: Principality of Phuan
description: The Principality of Phuan, historically known also as Muang Phuan and Tran Ninh, was an autonomous Lao highland state situated on the Xiangkhouang Plateau in north-eastern Laos. Governed from Muang Khoun by hereditary Phuan monarchs, the principality controlled valuable trade passes between the Mekong basin and northern Vietnam. The state preserved local self-government through shifting diplomatic alliances with Luang Phrabang and Dai Viet before falling under direct Siamese tributary hegemony in 1803. \n\n Status: Highland principality; Capital: Muang Khoun; Common languages: Phuan and Lao; Religion: Theravada Buddhism; Government: Hereditary principality; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1708; Disestablished: 1803; Preceded by: Lan Xang; Succeeded by: Phuan (Siamese tributary)

name: Akkalkot State
description: Akkalkot State was an autonomous Maratha princely realm situated on the Deccan plateau near the border of modern Maharashtra and Karnataka. Founded in 1708 by Ranoji Lokhande, who was adopted into the royal Bhonsle dynasty by Chhatrapati Shahu and granted the title of Fatehsinh Bhonsle, the state operated as a semi-autonomous fief within the Maratha Empire. The principality exercised local sovereign governance and fielded cavalry levies until British paramountcy consolidated the Deccan States Agency in 1849. \n\n Status: Princely state; Capital: Akkalkot; Common languages: Marathi and Kannada; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Princely monarchy; Ruler title: Raja; Ruling dynasty: Bhonsle; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1709; Disestablished: 1849; Succeeded by: Akkalkot (British protectorate)

name: Anomabu
description: Anomabu was an influential Fante coastal state situated along the Atlantic shoreline of modern-day Ghana. Operating from the fortified port town of Anomabu, the polity emerged as one of the pre-eminent trading centres on the Gold Coast, mediating maritime commerce between interior Akan producers and European merchants. The kingdom preserved its sovereign councils and merchant guilds throughout recurring conflicts with the Ashanti Empire until British colonial authorities formally annexed the territory into the Gold Coast colony in 1902. \n\n Status: Coastal kingdom; Capital: Anomabu; Common languages: Fante (Akan); Religion: Traditional African religion; Government: Elective chieftaincy; Ruler title: Omanhene; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1709; Disestablished: 1902; Succeeded by: British Gold Coast

name: State of the Presidi
label: holy roman empire
description: The State of the Presidi during this era was a coastal military possession held by the Austrian Habsburgs on the southern Tuscan coastline and the island of Elba. Comprising the strategic fortified enclaves of Orbetello, Porto Ercole, Porto Santo Stefano and Talamone, the territory was administered directly by the Austrian viceroy in Naples following the War of the Spanish Succession. The Habsburg administration garrisoned these naval outposts until Spanish Bourbon forces conquered Naples and its coastal dependencies in 1734. \n\n Status: Imperial coastal possession; Capital: Orbetello; Common languages: Italian; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Military governorship; Head of state: Charles VI; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1709; Disestablished: 1734; Preceded by: State of the Presidi (Spanish Habsburg); Succeeded by: State of the Presidi (Bourbon Naples)

name: Hotak Empire
description: The Hotak Empire was an Afghan monarchy established in April 1709 when Mirwais Hotak led a successful revolt of Ghilji Pashtun tribes against the Safavid governor of Kandahar. Expanding dramatically under Mahmud Hotak, the empire captured the Persian imperial capital of Isfahan in 1722 and deposed the Safavid shah, ruling large portions of Iran and southern Afghanistan. Internal dynastic instability and resurgent Persian armies under Nader Shah dismantled the empire, culminating in the fall of Kandahar in 1738. \n\n Status: Imperial monarchy; Capital: Kandahar; Common languages: Pashto and Persian; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Absolute monarchy; Ruler title: Emir; Head of state: Mirwais Hotak; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 21 April 1709; Disestablished: 1739; Succeeded by: Afsharid Empire

name: Principality of Soragna
label: holy roman empire
description: The Principality of Soragna was an immediate imperial territory of the Holy Roman Empire located in the fertile plains of Emilia-Romagna near Parma. Governed by the noble Meli Lupi dynasty from the fortified Rocca di Soragna, the historic marquisate was elevated to a sovereign principality by Emperor Joseph I on 4 August 1709 with the prerogative to mint coinage. The principality preserved its autonomous feudal governance until modernising administrative reforms and subsequent French revolutionary conquests dismantled imperial enclaves in northern Italy. \n\n Status: Imperial principality; Capital: Soragna; Common languages: Italian and Emilian; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Principality; Ruling dynasty: Meli Lupi; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 4 August 1709; Disestablished: 1792; Succeeded by: Duchy of Parma

name: Khanate of Kokand
description: The Khanate of Kokand was an autonomous Central Asian state established in the fertile Fergana Valley by Shahrukh Biy of the Uzbek Ming tribe following the fragmentation of the Bukhara Khanate. Governed from the fortified city of Kokand, the khanate fostered extensive irrigation systems, encouraged Silk Road caravan trade and unified sedentary Turkic and Persian-speaking urbanites with nomadic pastoralists. The realm asserted regional independence across eastern Central Asia until nineteenth-century imperial Russian military campaigns annexed the territory. \n\n Status: Sovereign khanate; Capital: Kokand; Common languages: Persian and Chagatai Turkic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Absolute monarchy; Ruler title: Khan; Ruling dynasty: Ming; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1710; Disestablished: 1 February 1867; Preceded by: Khanate of Bukhara; Succeeded by: Russian Empire

name: Kong Empire
description: The Kong Empire, also known as the Wattara Empire, was a powerful precolonial trading state centred at the commercial hub of Kong in north-eastern Ivory Coast. Established by Dyula Muslim merchants under Seku Wattara, the empire created a decentralised commercial network that protected long-distance trade routes connecting the Niger River basin with coastal forest belts. The empire maintained thriving textile industries and Islamic academies until the conqueror Samori Toure destroyed the capital in 1898 prior to French colonial occupation. \n\n Status: Commercial empire; Capital: Kong; Common languages: Dyula and Senufo; Religion: Islam and Traditional African religion; Government: Mercantile monarchy; Head of state: Seku Wattara; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1711; Disestablished: 1899; Succeeded by: French West Africa

name: Marquisate of Calice
label: holy roman empire
description: The Marquisate of Calice was a small immediate feudal fief of the Holy Roman Empire nestled in the mountainous Ligurian and Lunigiana hinterlands of north-western Italy. Governed by a cadet branch of the noble Malaspina family, the marquisate commanded defensive highland passes, managed timber forests and regulated local riverine tolls. The micro-territory exercised autonomous jurisdiction under imperial protection until dynastic negotiations and territorial restructuring led to its absorption by the Republic of Genoa in 1773. \n\n Status: Imperial marquisate; Capital: Calice; Common languages: Italian and Ligurian; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal marquisate; Ruling dynasty: Malaspina; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1711; Disestablished: 1773; Succeeded by: Republic of Genoa

name: Marquisate of Podenzana and Aulla
label: holy roman empire
description: The Marquisate of Podenzana and Aulla was an autonomous immediate estate of the Holy Roman Empire situated in the Lunigiana valley of northern Tuscany. Ruled by the Malaspina dello Spino Fiorito dynasty from the fortified castle of Podenzana, the lordship commanded strategic roads along the Magra River and maintained sovereign judicial prerogatives. The marquisate retained its feudal independence until the French revolutionary reorganisation of Italy abolished imperial fiefs through the Treaty of Campo Formio in October 1797. \n\n Status: Imperial marquisate; Capital: Podenzana; Common languages: Italian and Tuscan; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal marquisate; Ruling dynasty: Malaspina; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1711; Disestablished: 17 October 1797; Succeeded by: Cisalpine Republic

name: Nhowe
description: Nhowe was an autonomous precolonial Shona kingdom established across the granite hill country of Murewa in north-eastern Zimbabwe. Governed by the Mangwende dynasty from their mountain stronghold at Mahopo, the state operated an alternating collateral succession system between royal houses and maintained strong agrarian and pastoral traditions. The kingdom defended its sovereign territorial integrity against regional incursions until the British South Africa Company established colonial administrative control across Mashonaland in 1890. \n\n Status: Traditional kingdom; Capital: Mahopo; Common languages: Shona; Religion: Traditional African religion; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Ruler title: Mangwende; Ruling dynasty: Mangwende; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1711; Disestablished: 1890; Succeeded by: British South Africa Company

name: Tananarive Kingdom
description: The Tananarive Kingdom was an autonomous highland realm that arose in central Madagascar following the fourfold partition of the Merina kingdom by King Andriamasinavalona among his sons. Centred upon the fortified granite ridge of Antananarivo, the state commanded fertile rice valleys and defended its territory through fortified hill villages against neighbouring sibling kingdoms. Decades of internal strife ended when King Andrianampoinimerina of Ambohimanga captured Antananarivo in 1797, reunifying the central highlands into the unified Kingdom of Imerina. \n\n Status: Highland kingdom; Capital: Antananarivo; Common languages: Malagasy (Merina); Religion: Traditional Malagasy religion; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Ruler title: Mpanjaka; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1711; Disestablished: 1797; Preceded by: Kingdom of Imerina; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Imerina

name: Clipperton Island
description: Clipperton Island was an isolated French overseas maritime dependency comprising an uninhabited ring-shaped coral atoll in the north-eastern Pacific Ocean west of Mexico. Formally claimed for the French Crown by French naval explorers Martin de Chassiron and Michel Dubocage on Good Friday in April 1711, the territory provided a navigational benchmark and seasonal anchorage. Although uninhabited and subject to competing Mexican claims, French sovereignty was affirmed through international arbitration in 1931, preserving the atoll as a French state possession. \n\n Status: Overseas dependency; Capital: Clipperton Island; Common languages: French; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Colonial dependency; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 3 April 1711; Disestablished: 20 March 1986; Succeeded by: Clipperton Island (direct state property)

name: Principality of Schwarzburg-Rudolstadt
label: holy roman empire;confederation of the rhine;german confederation
description: The Principality of Schwarzburg-Rudolstadt was an autonomous German state of the Holy Roman Empire situated along the Saale River in the Thuringian Forest. Elevated to imperial princely rank on 15 April 1711 under Prince Louis Frederick I, the principality maintained an administrative capital at Rudolstadt and cultivated an active courtly life with thriving musical traditions. The state survived the dissolution of the Empire, joined the Confederation of the Rhine and the German Confederation, and eventually entered the German Empire in January 1871. \n\n Status: Imperial principality; Capital: Rudolstadt; Common languages: German; Religion: Lutheranism; Government: Principality; Ruler title: Prince; Head of state: Louis Frederick I; Legislature: Landtag; Historical era: Modern era; Established: 15 April 1711; Disestablished: 18 January 1871; Succeeded by: German Empire

name: Principality of Waldeck and Pyrmont
label: holy roman empire;confederation of the rhine;german confederation
description: The Principality of Waldeck and Pyrmont was an autonomous imperial principality of the Holy Roman Empire comprising the County of Waldeck in northern Hesse and the northern exclave of Bad Pyrmont. Elevated from an imperial county to a sovereign principality in 1712 by Emperor Charles VI under Prince Friedrich Anton Ulrich, the state was administered from the baroque residential palace at Arolsen. It preserved its constitutional autonomy through the Napoleonic period and the German Confederation before entering the unified German Empire in 1871. \n\n Status: Imperial principality; Capital: Arolsen; Common languages: German; Religion: Evangelical Protestantism; Government: Constitutional principality; Ruler title: Prince; Head of state: Friedrich Anton Ulrich; Historical era: Modern era; Established: 1712; Disestablished: 18 January 1871; Succeeded by: German Empire

name: Tripolitania Eyalet
description: The Tripolitania Eyalet during this era operated as a de facto independent maritime hereditary monarchy governed by the Karamanli dynasty under nominal Ottoman suzerainty. Established in 1711 when Ahmed Karamanli seized power in Tripoli and secured imperial recognition, the state financed its administration through Mediterranean privateering, trans-Saharan trade and maritime treaties with European powers. The dynasty extended its hegemony over Cyrenaica and the Fezzan until internal rebellions and naval pressures prompted the Ottoman Empire to restore direct rule in 1835. \n\n Status: Autonomous eyalet; Capital: Tripoli; Common languages: Arabic and Ottoman Turkish; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Hereditary pashalik; Ruler title: Pasha; Ruling dynasty: Karamanli; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1712; Disestablished: 1833; Succeeded by: Tripolitania Vilayet

name: Province of North Carolina
label: thirteen colonies
description: The Province of North Carolina was a British crown colony established in south-eastern North America following the formal administrative division of the proprietary Province of Carolina on 24 January 1712. Administered by a royal governor and an elected House of Burgesses from its provincial capital at New Bern, the colony developed an agrarian economy reliant on naval stores, tobacco and timber. The province exercised colonial self-government within the British Empire until renouncing royal authority during the American Revolution in 1776. \n\n Status: Crown colony; Capital: New Bern; Common languages: English; Religion: Anglicanism and Protestantism; Government: Colonial governorship; Legislature: General Assembly; Historical era: Georgian era; Established: 24 January 1712; Disestablished: 23 December 1776; Preceded by: Province of Carolina; Succeeded by: State of North Carolina

name: Province of South Carolina
label: thirteen colonies
description: The Province of South Carolina was a British crown colony created on 24 January 1712 when the Carolina proprietorship was partitioned into distinct northern and southern administrations. Centred upon the thriving Atlantic port of Charleston, the colony developed a lucrative plantation economy heavily reliant on enslaved labour to produce rice and indigo. South Carolina maintained a bicameral assembly and royal governorship until revolutionary delegates repudiated British imperial governance in 1776 to join the nascent American republic. \n\n Status: Crown colony; Capital: Charleston; Common languages: English; Religion: Anglicanism; Government: Colonial governorship; Legislature: General Assembly; Historical era: Georgian era; Established: 24 January 1712; Disestablished: 23 December 1776; Preceded by: Province of Carolina; Succeeded by: State of South Carolina

name: Kingdom of Poland and the Grand Duchy of Lithuania, Denmark-Norway and Tsardom of Russia (Military Occupation)
description: The joint military occupation conducted by the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, Denmark-Norway and the Tsardom of Russia encompassed captured Swedish territories around the southern Baltic coast during the Great Northern War. Operating under an allied tripartite military council, coalition forces laid siege to Swedish Pomerania, captured the fortified port of Stralsund and secured coastal supply lines. The allied military administration governed local districts provisionally until the peace congresses of Stockholm and Frederiksborg reallocated Baltic jurisdictions in 1720. \n\n Status: Allied military occupation; Capital: None (decentralised); Common languages: German, Danish, Polish and Russian; Religion: Lutheranism and Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Joint military council; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1 June 1712; Disestablished: 14 July 1720; Succeeded by: Prussian Pomerania

name: Electorate of Hanover (Military Occupation)
label: holy roman empire
description: The Electorate of Hanover military occupation was an emergency wartime administration established by the forces of Brunswick-Lüneburg across northern German territories during the Great Northern War and Seven Years' War. Hanoverian troops occupied the Swedish-held duchies of Bremen and Verden to safeguard northern river corridors along the Weser and Elbe from foreign incursions. The military governorate administered local taxation, garrisons and civilian provisioning until diplomatic purchases and treaties transferred formal sovereignty to the Hanoverian Crown. \n\n Status: Military occupation; Capital: None (decentralised); Common languages: German and Low German; Religion: Lutheranism; Government: Military administration; Head of state: George I Louis; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1 October 1712; Disestablished: 2 May 1715; Succeeded by: Duchies of Bremen and Verden

name: Bamana Empire
description: The Bamana Empire, also known as the Segou Empire, was a powerful West African state established in the middle Niger River basin of modern-day Mali. Founded by Biton Mamary Coulibaly, who organised an elite standing army of professional soldiers known as the tonjon, the empire expanded across the Sahel through centralised military administration and control of riverine commerce. The realm flourished as an agrarian and commercial power until it was conquered in March 1861 by the Toucouleur army of El Hadj Umar Tall. \n\n Status: Imperial monarchy; Capital: Ségou; Common languages: Bambara; Religion: Traditional African religion and Islam; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Faama; Head of state: Biton Coulibaly; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1713; Disestablished: 10 March 1861; Succeeded by: Toucouleur Empire

name: Duchies of Bremen and Verden
label: holy roman empire
description: The Duchies of Bremen and Verden during this period functioned as an imperial territory under Danish military occupation and governance following their capture from the Swedish Crown during the Great Northern War. Administered from the fortress city of Stade, the provincial government maintained local Lutheran ecclesiastical institutions while collecting customs duties along the lower Weser and Elbe rivers. Danish authorities managed the territory until negotiating its formal transfer and sale to the Electorate of Hanover. \n\n Status: Occupied imperial duchies; Capital: Stade; Common languages: German and Low Saxon; Religion: Lutheranism; Government: Military governorship; Head of state: Frederick IV; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1713; Disestablished: 1787; Preceded by: Bremen-Verden (Swedish); Succeeded by: Electorate of Hanover

name: Principality of Liechtenstein
label: holy roman empire;confederation of the rhine;german confederation
description: The Principality of Liechtenstein is a landlocked alpine microstate situated between Austria and Switzerland along the upper Rhine valley. Created as an immediate imperial principality of the Holy Roman Empire through the purchase and elevation of the Lordship of Schellenberg and County of Vaduz by the princely House of Liechtenstein, the state secured sovereign status in the Imperial Diet. The principality preserved its independence through the dissolution of the Empire, the German Confederation and modern European integration. \n\n Status: Sovereign principality; Capital: Vaduz; Official languages: German; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Constitutional monarchy; Ruler title: Prince of Liechtenstein; Legislature: Landtag; Historical era: Modern era; Established: 1713; Preceded by: County of Vaduz and Lordship of Schellenberg

name: Tamatave Kingdom
description: The Tamatave Kingdom was an autonomous coastal state situated around the major seaport of Toamasina on the eastern shoreline of Madagascar. Governed by local Betsimisaraka chieftains and merchant dynasties, the realm developed as a crucial Indian Ocean trading hub connecting highland Malagasy communities with French and British maritime merchants. The kingdom retained independent authority over coastal harbours and regional commerce until the military expansion of King Radama I incorporated Tamatave into the Kingdom of Imerina in 1818. \n\n Status: Coastal kingdom; Capital: Toamasina; Common languages: Malagasy; Religion: Traditional Malagasy religion; Government: Traditional monarchy; Ruler title: Mpanjaka; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1713; Disestablished: 1818; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Imerina

name: Gibraltar
description: Gibraltar is a British overseas territory occupying a fortified limestone promontory on the southern coast of the Iberian Peninsula commanding the entrance to the Mediterranean Sea. Captured by an Anglo-Dutch fleet in 1704 during the War of the Spanish Succession, the garrison and its port were formally ceded in perpetuity to Great Britain by the Crown of Spain under the Treaty of Utrecht in April 1713. The strategic outpost developed into a pivotal Royal Navy maritime base and maintained continuous British administration. \n\n Status: Overseas territory; Capital: Gibraltar; Official languages: English; Common languages: English and Spanish; Religion: Roman Catholicism and Anglicanism; Government: Parliamentary dependency; Legislature: Parliament; Historical era: Modern era; Established: 11 April 1713; Preceded by: Crown of Castile

name: Kingdom of Sicily
description: The Kingdom of Sicily during this period was ruled by Duke Victor Amadeus II of the House of Savoy, who was awarded the island kingdom and royal dignity under the Treaty of Utrecht in April 1713. Administered from Palermo, the Savoyard monarchy attempted administrative modernisations, reformed island finances and asserted royal prerogatives over the Sicilian barony. Following Spanish military invasion and subsequent quadripartite diplomacy, Savoy exchanged Sicily for Sardinia with the Austrian Habsburgs under the Treaty of The Hague in 1720. \n\n Status: Royal possession; Capital: Palermo; Common languages: Sicilian and Italian; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Monarchy; Head of state: Victor Amadeus II; Ruler title: King of Sicily; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 11 April 1713; Disestablished: 6 May 1720; Preceded by: Kingdom of Sicily (Spanish Habsburg); Succeeded by: Kingdom of Sicily (Austrian Habsburg)

name: Minorca
description: Minorca was a British crown colony in the western Mediterranean comprising the second-largest of the Balearic Islands. Captured by Anglo-Dutch expeditionary forces in 1708, the island was formally ceded to Great Britain by Spain under the Treaty of Utrecht in April 1713 due to the strategic value of its deep-water harbour at Port Mahon. British governors established naval dockyards and garrisons across the island, administering the territory through the eighteenth century with brief interruptions during Franco-Spanish wartime occupations. \n\n Status: Crown colony; Capital: Ciutadella de Menorca; Common languages: Catalan (Menorqui), Spanish and English; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Colonial governorship; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 11 April 1713; Disestablished: 5 February 1782; Preceded by: Crown of Aragon; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Spain

name: Saint Pierre and Miquelon
description: Saint Pierre and Miquelon was a British colonial island possession situated off the Burin Peninsula of southern Newfoundland in the North Atlantic Ocean. Ceded by France to Great Britain under the Treaty of Utrecht in April 1713 following the War of the Spanish Succession, the archipelago served as an important offshore base for seasonal cod fisheries and naval patrols. The islands were subject to repeated wartime captures and diplomatic restitutions between Britain and France before permanently returning to French administration in 1816. \n\n Status: Crown colony; Capital: None (decentralised); Common languages: English and French; Religion: Roman Catholicism and Protestantism; Government: Colonial administration; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 11 April 1713; Disestablished: 22 June 1816; Preceded by: French North America; Succeeded by: French Saint Pierre and Miquelon

name: Kingdom of Poland and the Grand Duchy of Lithuania and Tsardom of Russia (Military Occupation)
description: The joint military occupation conducted by the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth and the Tsardom of Russia was a brief wartime administration established following the allied capture of the Swedish fortress of Stettin in September 1713. Coalition forces under Prince Alexander Menshikov took control of the strategic Pomeranian redoubt at the mouth of the Oder River during the Great Northern War. The provisional allied regime concluded within weeks when diplomatic accords transferred control of Stettin to neutral Prussian sequestration forces. \n\n Status: Allied military occupation; Capital: None (decentralised); Common languages: German, Polish and Russian; Religion: Lutheranism and Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Joint military command; Head of state: Peter I and Augustus II; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 19 September 1713; Disestablished: 6 October 1713; Succeeded by: Prussian Stettin

name: Kingdom of Champasak
description: The Kingdom of Champasak, also known historically as Bassac, was an autonomous Lao kingdom established in southern Laos in 1713 amidst the dissolution of the Lan Xang Empire. Ruled from its riverine capital on the lower Mekong River by King Nokasad, a grandson of King Sourigna Vongsa, the state commanded lucrative trade across the Bolaven Plateau and southern waterways. Champasak maintained its sovereign domestic independence until Siamese military forces under Chao Phraya Chakri conquered the realm in 1778 and 1779. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Champasak; Common languages: Lao; Religion: Theravada Buddhism; Government: Absolute monarchy; Ruler title: King; Head of state: Nokasad; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1714; Disestablished: 1779; Preceded by: Lan Xang; Succeeded by: Champasak (Siamese vassal)

name: Sandur State
description: Sandur State was an autonomous Maratha princely realm situated in a rugged mountain valley in the Bellary region of modern-day eastern Karnataka. Founded in 1713 by Sidhoji Rao Ghorpade, an esteemed Maratha military general, the dynasty governed from the hill-ringed settlement of Sandur and derived revenue from fertile valley agriculture and mineral deposits. The state defended its independence against neighbouring Mysore and Hyderabad armies before entering into a subsidiary alliance with the British East India Company in 1818. \n\n Status: Princely state; Capital: Sandur; Common languages: Marathi and Kannada; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Princely monarchy; Ruler title: Raja; Ruling dynasty: Ghorpade; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1714; Disestablished: 7 January 1818; Succeeded by: Sandur (British protectorate)

name: Kingdom of Naples
description: The Kingdom of Naples during this period was ruled in personal union by the Austrian Habsburg emperor Charles VI following the partition of the Spanish Empire ratified by the Treaties of Utrecht and Rastatt. Governed by appointed imperial viceroys in the capital of Naples, the administration attempted fiscal reorganisations and curbed the autonomous privileges of the local feudal nobility and Catholic clergy. Austrian rule ended in November 1734 when Spanish Bourbon troops under the infante Don Carlos conquered the kingdom during the War of the Polish Succession. \n\n Status: Kingdom in personal union; Capital: Naples; Common languages: Neapolitan and Italian; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Monarchy; Head of state: Charles VI; Ruler title: King of Naples; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 7 March 1714; Disestablished: 30 November 1734; Preceded by: Kingdom of Naples (Spanish Habsburg); Succeeded by: Kingdom of Naples (Bourbon)

name: Kingdom of Sardinia
description: The Kingdom of Sardinia during this phase was held as an insular possession of the Austrian Habsburgs following the European settlements of the Treaties of Utrecht and Rastatt in 1714. Governed from the coastal capital of Cagliari by an imperial viceroy representing Emperor Charles VI, the administration attempted to secure island defences and maintain customary Sardinian legal privileges. Habsburg control was abruptly terminated in September 1717 when a Spanish naval expedition recaptured the island during the War of the Quadruple Alliance. \n\n Status: Imperial possession; Capital: Cagliari; Common languages: Sardinian, Catalan, Spanish and Italian; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Viceroyalty; Head of state: Charles VI; Ruler title: King of Sardinia; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 7 March 1714; Disestablished: 1 September 1717; Preceded by: Kingdom of Sardinia (Spanish Habsburg); Succeeded by: Kingdom of Sardinia (Spanish occupation)

name: Electorate of Hanover
description: The Electorate of Hanover, officially the Electorate of Brunswick-Lüneburg, was an imperial state of the Holy Roman Empire ruled in personal union with the Kingdom of Great Britain from 1 August 1714. Following the Hanoverian Succession of Elector George Louis as King George I, the electorate maintained its distinct constitutional identity, civil laws and Privy Council in Hanover. The realm expanded its northern territories until being overrun during the Napoleonic Wars and subsequently elevated to the Kingdom of Hanover at the Congress of Vienna. \n\n Status: Electorate in personal union; Capital: Hannover; Common languages: German and Low German; Religion: Lutheranism; Government: Constitutional principality; Ruler title: Prince-elector; Head of state: George I; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1 August 1714; Disestablished: 12 October 1814; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Hanover

name: Gwiriko
description: Gwiriko was an autonomous West African kingdom established in the fertile upper Banifin and Volta river basins in south-western Burkina Faso. Founded by Famagan Ouattara as an offshoot of the Kong Empire, the realm made Bobo-Dioulasso its political and commercial centre, fostering extensive trade networks between northern savannahs and southern forests. The kingdom preserved its sovereign decentralised institutions despite frequent Tieba and Samorian conflicts until French colonial forces occupied the region in 1897 and 1898. \n\n Status: Traditional kingdom; Capital: Bobo-Dioulasso; Common languages: Dyula and Bobo; Religion: Islam and Traditional African religion; Government: Traditional monarchy; Head of state: Famagan Ouattara; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1715; Disestablished: 1898; Preceded by: Kong Empire; Succeeded by: French West Africa

name: Kingdom of Spain
description: The Kingdom of Spain emerged as a unified, centralised national monarchy following the promulgation of the Nueva Planta decrees by the Bourbon king Philip V between 1707 and 1716. Abolishing the autonomous crown institutions of Aragon, Catalonia and Valencia, the monarchy centralised imperial administration and taxation in Madrid along French administrative models. Spain governed extensive global territories across the Americas and the Philippines through the eighteenth century and remains a sovereign European parliamentary monarchy today. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Madrid; Official languages: Spanish; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Parliamentary constitutional monarchy; Ruler title: King of Spain; Legislature: Cortes Generales; Historical era: Modern era; Established: 9 June 1715; Preceded by: Crown of Castile and Crown of Aragon

name: Kingdom of Poland and the Grand Duchy of Lithuania, Denmark-Norway and Kingdom of Prussia (Military Occupation)
description: The joint military occupation administered by the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, Denmark-Norway and the Kingdom of Prussia was an allied wartime command formed to capture and govern Swedish exclaves in northern Germany during the Great Northern War. Allied forces besieged the fortified Swedish port of Wismar, dismantled its perimeter fortifications and provisioned occupation garrisons across coastal Mecklenburg. The coalition administration ended following the Treaty of Frederiksborg and related settlements that restored civil governance in 1720. \n\n Status: Allied military occupation; Capital: None (decentralised); Common languages: German, Danish and Polish; Religion: Lutheranism; Government: Allied military council; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 11 June 1715; Disestablished: 14 July 1720; Succeeded by: Swedish Wismar

name: Isle de France
description: Isle de France was a French crown colony comprising the Indian Ocean island now known as Mauritius along with outlying island dependencies such as Rodrigues and the Chagos Archipelago. Administered initially by the French East India Company and subsequently by royal governors from Port Louis, the colony developed extensive sugar plantations worked by enslaved labourers and served as a formidable naval station. French corsairs and naval squadrons operated from the island during the Napoleonic Wars until British expeditionary forces captured it in December 1810. \n\n Status: Overseas colony; Capital: Port Louis; Common languages: French and Mauritian Creole; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Colonial governorship; Head of state: Louis XV; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1716; Disestablished: 3 December 1810; Preceded by: Dutch Mauritius; Succeeded by: British Mauritius

name: Mandara Sultanate
description: The Mandara Sultanate, also known historically as Wandala, was an autonomous kingdom established in the Mandara Mountains of northern Cameroon. Following the official conversion of King Mai Bukar Aji to Islam around 1715, the state transformed its political structure into a sultanate and shifted its royal residence to Mora. The realm commanded vital regional trade in iron, textiles and horses, maintaining its independence against Bornu and the Sokoto Caliphate until German colonial forces subdued the region in 1902 and 1903. \n\n Status: Traditional sultanate; Capital: Mora; Common languages: Wandala; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Sultan (Mai); Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1716; Disestablished: 1903; Succeeded by: German Cameroon

name: Domain of Jan Conny
description: The Domain of Jan Conny was an autonomous indigenous African polity established along the western Gold Coast of Ghana by the Ahanta warrior-merchant Jan Conny, also known as John Canoe. Following the Prussian abandonment of Fort Gross Friedrichsburg at Princes Town, Conny seized the coastal fortification and commanded an armed force of local warriors to control maritime commerce. He successfully defied Dutch, English and Prussian naval expeditions for nearly a decade until a large Dutch military assault captured the fortress in 1725. \n\n Status: Autonomous domain; Capital: Princess Town; Common languages: Ahanta and Akan; Religion: Traditional African religion; Government: Military chieftaincy; Head of state: Jan Conny; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1717; Disestablished: 1725; Preceded by: Prussian Gold Coast; Succeeded by: Dutch Gold Coast

name: Sailana State
description: Sailana State was an autonomous Rajput princely state established in the Malwa region of central India by Raja Jai Singh, a great-grandson of Ratan Singh of Ratlam. Ruling from the capital of Sailana, the Rathore dynasty maintained local armed garrisons, collected land revenues and preserved independence amidst the disintegration of the Mughal Empire and Maratha expansion. The state retained full internal sovereignty until concluding a subsidiary alliance treaty with the British East India Company in May 1819. \n\n Status: Princely state; Capital: Sailana; Common languages: Malvi and Hindi; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Princely monarchy; Ruler title: Raja; Ruling dynasty: Rathore; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1717; Disestablished: 1 May 1819; Succeeded by: Sailana (British protectorate)

name: Great Jüz
description: The Great Jüz, or Ulu Jüz, was an autonomous nomadic tribal union of the Kazakh people that controlled the pastures and trade routes of the Jetysu and Syr Darya basins in south-eastern Kazakhstan. Following the death of Tauke Khan and the fragmentation of the unified Kazakh Khanate, the confederation was governed by its own elected khan and tribal biys from historic centres like Turkistan. The confederacy defended its southern frontiers against Dzungar incursions and maintained independence until accepting Qing and later Russian imperial protection. \n\n Status: Nomadic confederation; Capital: Turkistan; Common languages: Kazakh; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Semi-elective nomadic monarchy; Ruler title: Khan; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1719; Disestablished: 1772; Preceded by: Kazakh Khanate; Succeeded by: Great Jüz (Qing tributary)

name: Little Jüz
description: The Little Jüz, or Kishi Jüz, was an autonomous nomadic confederation of Kazakh pastoralist clans that roamed the vast dry steppes between the lower Volga, the Ural River and the Aral Sea in western Kazakhstan. Emerging as an independent entity after the death of Tauke Khan under the leadership of Abulkhair Khan, the confederation maintained a mobile court without a permanent fixed capital. Facing destructive raids from Kalmyk and Dzungar neighbours, the Little Jüz balanced nomadic independence with diplomatic appeals to the Russian Empire. \n\n Status: Nomadic confederation; Capital: None (decentralised); Common languages: Kazakh; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Elective pastoral khanate; Ruler title: Khan; Head of state: Abulkhair Khan; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1719; Disestablished: 1772; Preceded by: Kazakh Khanate; Succeeded by: Little Jüz (Russian protectorate)

name: Middle Jüz
description: The Middle Jüz, or Orta Jüz, was the largest of the three autonomous nomadic confederations of the Kazakh people, roaming the expansive plains of central and north-eastern Kazakhstan. Emerging after the splintering of the unified Kazakh Khanate, the union was led by influential khans such as Semeke and later Ablai Khan who operated from seasonal nomadic encampments without a fixed urban seat. The confederacy waged defensive campaigns against the Dzungar Khanate while skilfully balancing diplomatic relations between the Russian and Qing empires. \n\n Status: Nomadic confederation; Capital: None (decentralised); Common languages: Kazakh; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Elective pastoral khanate; Ruler title: Khan; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1719; Disestablished: 1772; Preceded by: Kazakh Khanate; Succeeded by: Middle Jüz (Qing and Russian tributary)

name: Mughal Empire
description: The Mughal Empire during this era functioned as a diminished imperial protectorate under the paramount military authority of the Maratha Empire. Following the deposition of Emperor Farrukhsiyar in 1719 and subsequent Maratha military ascendance across northern India, the Mughal emperors in Delhi were reduced to figureheads whose security and revenue collections depended on Maratha peshwas and generals. The protectorate arrangement endured until British East India Company forces decisively defeated the Maratha Confederacy in 1818 and established direct paramountcy over Delhi. \n\n Status: Imperial protectorate; Capital: Delhi; Official languages: Persian; Common languages: Hindustani and Persian; Religion: Sunni Islam and Hinduism; Government: Monarchy under Maratha protection; Ruler title: Emperor; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1720; Disestablished: 1 May 1819; Preceded by: Mughal Empire (sovereign); Succeeded by: Mughal Empire (British protectorate)

name: Saint Vincent
description: Saint Vincent was a French colonial island possession situated in the Windward Islands of the south-eastern Caribbean Sea. Following initial French settlement from Martinique around 1719, French planters established coffee, cocoa and indigo plantations along the coast while negotiating precarious coexistence with the indigenous Garifuna and Island Carib populations. French administrative and commercial control endured until British expeditionary forces captured Kingstown in March 1762 during the Seven Years' War, leading to formal cession under the Treaty of Paris. \n\n Status: Overseas colony; Capital: Kingstown; Common languages: French and Vincentian Creole; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Colonial governorship; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1720; Disestablished: 3 March 1762; Preceded by: Indigenous Island Carib domain; Succeeded by: British Saint Vincent

name: Kingdom of Sardinia
description: The Kingdom of Sardinia during this transitional phase was an insular possession acquired by Duke Victor Amadeus II of Savoy under the Treaty of The Hague on 17 February 1720 in exchange for Sicily. The Savoyard administration established vice-regal authority over the island from Cagliari, confirming customary local laws while preparing to integrate the realm with their continental possessions in Piedmont and Savoy. This brief period of separate insular administration laid the groundwork for the unified Savoyard Kingdom of Sardinia. \n\n Status: Royal possession; Capital: Cagliari; Common languages: Sardinian, Catalan, Italian and French; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Viceroyalty; Head of state: Victor Amadeus II; Ruler title: King of Sardinia; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 17 February 1720; Disestablished: 1721; Preceded by: Kingdom of Sardinia (Spanish Habsburg); Succeeded by: Kingdom of Sardinia (Savoyard state)

name: Kingdom of Sicily
description: The Kingdom of Sicily during this period was an insular royal possession ruled by Emperor Charles VI of the Austrian Habsburg dynasty following the Treaty of The Hague in 1720. Governed from Palermo by an appointed imperial viceroy, the Austrian administration reorganised Sicilian taxation, restructured coastal defence against Barbary corsairs and contended with recalcitrant baronial assemblies. Habsburg rule ended in October 1734 when Spanish Bourbon armies under the Duke of Montemar successfully invaded the island during the War of the Polish Succession. \n\n Status: Imperial royal possession; Capital: Palermo; Common languages: Sicilian and Italian; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Viceroyalty; Head of state: Charles VI; Ruler title: King of Sicily; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 6 May 1720; Disestablished: 1 October 1734; Preceded by: Kingdom of Sicily (Savoyard); Succeeded by: Kingdom of Sicily (Bourbon)

name: Principality of Lippe
label: holy roman empire;confederation of the rhine;german confederation
description: The Principality of Lippe, also known as Lippe-Detmold, was an autonomous imperial state of the Holy Roman Empire situated in Westphalia between the Weser River and the Teutoburg Forest. Ruled from the residential town of Detmold by the House of Lippe, the state maintained a Calvinist ecclesiastical establishment and developed an agrarian economy supported by local timber and textile industries. The principality preserved its sovereignty through the Napoleonic period and the German Confederation before becoming a constituent state of the German Empire in January 1871. \n\n Status: Imperial principality; Capital: Detmold; Common languages: German and West Low German; Religion: Calvinism; Government: Constitutional principality; Ruler title: Prince of Lippe; Legislature: Landtag; Historical era: Modern era; Established: 27 October 1720; Disestablished: 18 January 1871; Succeeded by: German Empire

name: Ganden Phodrang
description: Ganden Phodrang was the traditional Tibetan theocratic government headed by the Dalai Lamas from the Potala Palace in Lhasa, operating as a tributary vassal under the suzerainty of the Qing dynasty of China. Following the expulsion of Dzungar invaders by Qing imperial armies in 1720, the Qing court stationed imperial residents known as ambans in Lhasa and oversaw external defence and frontier diplomacy while leaving domestic administration to Tibetan ecclesiastical regents and the Kashag council. This autonomous protectorate lasted until Qing military occupation in 1910. \n\n Status: Tributary theocracy; Capital: Lhasa; Common languages: Tibetan and Manchu; Religion: Tibetan Buddhism; Government: Theocratic monarchy; Ruler title: Dalai Lama; Established: 1721; Disestablished: 25 February 1910

name: Kingdom of Kooki
label: african great lakes kingdoms
description: The Kingdom of Kooki was an autonomous precolonial Great Lakes state situated in what is now Rakai District in southern Uganda. Established by migrating princes of the Babiito royal lineage from Bunyoro-Kitara, the kingdom was ruled by a hereditary monarch styled the Kamuswaga and grew wealthy through iron production, pottery and regional trade between Lake Victoria and the western kingdoms. Facing military pressure from neighbouring Buganda in the late nineteenth century, the Kamuswaga signed an agreement in 1896 that incorporated Kooki into the British Protectorate of Buganda. \n\n Status: Great Lakes kingdom; Capital: Rakai; Common languages: Luganda; Religion: Traditional African religion; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Ruler title: Kamuswaga; Established: 1721; Disestablished: 1897

name: Kingdom of Sardinia
label: holy roman empire
description: The Kingdom of Sardinia, often called Piedmont-Sardinia, was a sovereign Italian realm governed by the House of Savoy with its political and administrative capital at Turin. Combining the island of Sardinia with the mainland territories of Piedmont, Savoy and the County of Nice, the kingdom developed a modernised military, an efficient civil bureaucracy and extensive industrial infrastructure. In the nineteenth century, Sardinia led the Risorgimento movement for Italian national unification, culminating in the proclamation of the Kingdom of Italy on 17 March 1861. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Torino; Official languages: Italian and French; Common languages: Piedmontese, Sardinian, Italian and French; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Constitutional monarchy; Ruler title: King of Sardinia; Legislature: Parliament; Historical era: Modern era; Established: 1721; Disestablished: 17 March 1861; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Italy

name: Nafana
description: Nafana was an autonomous precolonial state established by Senufo-speaking communities in the savanna borderlands of north-eastern Ivory Coast and north-western Ghana around Bondoukou. Originating from historic migrations linked to the decline of Songhai, the realm established thriving farming communities and gold-trading networks in close commercial contact with neighbouring Dyula and Ligbi merchants. The polity maintained independent local governance until expanding Ashanti armies brought the Banda and Nafana territories under imperial vassalage in 1816. \n\n Status: Traditional chieftaincy; Capital: Bondoukou; Common languages: Nafaanra; Religion: Traditional African religion; Government: Traditional chieftaincy; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1721; Disestablished: 1816; Succeeded by: Ashanti Empire

name: Nagod State
description: Nagod State, historically known as Unchahara, was an autonomous Rajput princely realm situated in the Satna region of modern-day Madhya Pradesh in central India. Ruled by the Parihar Rajput dynasty, the principality shifted its administrative seat from Unchehara to Nagod in the early eighteenth century while defending its territory against neighbouring Bundela and Maratha forces. The state governed its agrarian estates with local autonomy until entering into formal subsidiary relations with the British East India Company in the early nineteenth century. \n\n Status: Princely state; Capital: Nagod; Common languages: Bundeli and Hindi; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Princely monarchy; Ruler title: Raja; Ruling dynasty: Parihar; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1721; Disestablished: 1821; Succeeded by: Nagod (British protectorate)

name: Sefwi-Wiawso
description: Sefwi-Wiawso was an autonomous Akan kingdom established in the dense rainforests of western Ghana along the Tano River basin. Governed from the hilltop capital of Sefwi Wiawso by a paramount ruler bearing the title Omanhene, the realm prospered through extensive gold panning, timber harvesting and agricultural production. The kingdom preserved its independence through shifting alliances and defensive wars against neighbouring Denkyira and Ashanti armies until British colonial authorities incorporated the area into the Gold Coast Protectorate in 1902. \n\n Status: Traditional kingdom; Capital: Sefwi Wiawso; Common languages: Sefwi and Twi; Religion: Traditional African religion; Government: Elective chieftaincy; Ruler title: Omanhene; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1721; Disestablished: 1902; Succeeded by: British Gold Coast

name: Russian Empire
description: The Russian Empire was proclaimed on 2 November 1721 by Peter the Great following victory over Sweden in the Great Northern War, transforming the Tsardom of Russia into a transcontinental great power. Spanning from the Baltic Sea across northern Eurasia to the Pacific Ocean, the empire established its administrative seat at Saint Petersburg and created modernised civil, military and scientific institutions. The autocracy expanded under Catherine the Great and Alexander I, remaining one of the world's largest empires until the Russian Revolution overthrew the monarchy in 1917. \n\n Status: Sovereign empire; Capital: Saint Petersburg; Official languages: Russian; Religion: Russian Orthodoxy; Government: Absolute monarchy; Ruler title: Emperor of All Russia; Established: 2 November 1721; Disestablished: 14 September 1917

name: Banda
description: Banda was an autonomous precolonial trading kingdom situated in the transition zone between savannah and forest in the north-western Bono Region of Ghana. Inhabited by Nafana, Ligbi and Bono peoples, the state prospered as an overland trade terminus facilitating exchanges of gold, kola nuts, salt and textiles between the Sahelian networks and the Guinea coast. The kingdom defended its political independence until the military campaigns of the expanding Ashanti Empire brought the territory under tributary subjugation in 1751. \n\n Status: Traditional kingdom; Capital: None (decentralised); Common languages: Nafaanra and Bono (Akan); Religion: Traditional African religion and Islam; Government: Chieftaincy; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1722; Disestablished: 1751; Succeeded by: Ashanti Empire

name: Baroda State
description: Baroda State was an autonomous Maratha realm established across Gujarat in western India by Pilaji Rao Gaekwad during the territorial fragmentation of the Mughal province of Gujarat. Operating from the fortified capital of Baroda, the Gaekwad dynasty maintained a formidable cavalry army, collected chauth revenues and established administrative control over fertile coastal plains and inland agricultural tracts. The state acted as a sovereign power within the Maratha Confederacy until concluding the Treaty of Baroda with the British East India Company in 1805 and 1806. \n\n Status: Princely state; Capital: Vadodara; Common languages: Gujarati and Marathi; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Princely monarchy; Ruler title: Maharaja; Ruling dynasty: Gaekwad; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1722; Disestablished: 1806; Preceded by: Maratha Empire; Succeeded by: Baroda (British subsidiary alliance)

name: Souliotes
description: The Souliotes constituted an autonomous warrior confederation of Christian Albanian clans who settled in the remote, mountainous highlands of Souli in Epirus in north-western Greece. Organised into four main mountain villages known as the Tetrachori, the community governed itself through a council of clan elders, successfully rebuffing repeated Ottoman expeditions and dominating neighbouring agrarian valleys. The confederacy's protracted armed resistance against Ali Pasha of Yanina culminated in the siege and fall of Souli in December 1803, forcing the surviving fighters into exile. \n\n Status: Autonomous tribal confederation; Capital: Souli; Common languages: Souliotic Albanian and Greek; Religion: Greek Orthodoxy; Government: Clan confederacy; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1722; Disestablished: 7 December 1803; Succeeded by: Ottoman Empire

name: Russian Empire (Military Occupation)
description: The Russian Empire military occupation during this initial phase encompassed imperial administration established over conquered Caspian littoral provinces during the Russo-Persian War of 1722 to 1723. Under the personal command of Emperor Peter the Great, Russian naval and land forces occupied the strategic Caspian fortresses of Derbent, Baku and Rasht in northern Persia. Imperial military governors administered these coastal territories provisionally to secure trade routes to India until diplomatic treaties restored the southern Caspian provinces to Persia in the 1730s. \n\n Status: Imperial military occupation; Capital: None (decentralised); Common languages: Russian, Persian and Azerbaijani; Religion: Russian Orthodoxy and Islam; Government: Military administration; Head of state: Peter I; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 7 August 1722; Disestablished: 1726; Succeeded by: Safavid Empire

name: Al Qasimi Domain
description: The Al Qasimi Domain was a powerful maritime Arab confederation ruled by the Qasimi dynasty, commanding the strategic waters of the Persian Gulf and Gulf of Oman from fortified ports at Ras Al Khaimah and Sharjah. Possessing a formidable fleet of ocean-going dhows, the confederation dominated regional coastal trade, collected maritime duties and contested naval supremacy with the Sultanate of Muscat and Oman. British naval expeditions attacked Qasimi ports in 1809 and 1819, leading to the General Maritime Treaty of 1820 that established the Trucial States. \n\n Status: Maritime emirate; Capital: Ras Al Khaimah; Common languages: Arabic; Religion: Sunni Islam (Wahhabi influence); Government: Traditional monarchy; Ruler title: Sheikh; Ruling dynasty: Al Qasimi; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1723; Disestablished: 5 February 1820; Succeeded by: Trucial States

name: Ostend Company
description: The Ostend Company was a chartered overseas trading company established in the Austrian Netherlands in 1722 under a patent granted by Holy Roman Emperor Charles VI. Operating primarily from the Flemish port of Ostend, the enterprise founded prosperous trading factories at Bankipur in Bengal and Cabelon on the Coromandel Coast of India, competing directly in the lucrative tea and silk trade. British and Dutch diplomatic pressure forced Emperor Charles VI to suspend and dismantle the company in exchange for international recognition of the Pragmatic Sanction. \n\n Status: Chartered company rule; Capital: Oostende; Common languages: Dutch, French and German; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Corporate board; Head of state: Charles VI; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1723; Disestablished: 1734; Succeeded by: Austrian Netherlands

name: Banana Islands
label: english chieftancies in sierra leone
description: The Banana Islands comprised an autonomous insular chiefdom situated off the coast of Yawri Bay south-west of the Freetown Peninsula in modern Sierra Leone. Ruled by prominent Afro-European merchant-chief dynasties such as the Caulkers and Clevelands, the islands served as a secure maritime trading depot for ivory, camwood and provisions for Atlantic merchant vessels. The chiefdom maintained independent local governance until Chief Thomas Caulker ceded the islands to the British Crown on 21 July 1820, integrating them into colonial Sierra Leone. \n\n Status: Island chiefdom; Capital: Dublin; Common languages: Krio, Mende and English; Religion: Traditional African religion and Protestantism; Government: Chieftaincy; Ruling dynasty: Caulker; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1724; Disestablished: 21 July 1820; Succeeded by: British Sierra Leone

name: Bhavnagar State
description: Bhavnagar State was an autonomous Rajput princely realm founded on the eastern coast of the Kathiawar peninsula in Gujarat by Bhavsinhji I of the Gohil clan in 1723. Developing the new deep-water port of Bhavnagar as its capital, the state established maritime commerce with the Persian Gulf, built naval defences against pirates and managed fertile agricultural lands in Saurashtra. The state operated as an independent regional power until entering into subsidiary treaty relationships with the British East India Company in 1808. \n\n Status: Princely state; Capital: Bhavnagar; Common languages: Gujarati; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Princely monarchy; Ruler title: Thakur Sahib; Ruling dynasty: Gohil; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1724; Disestablished: 1808; Succeeded by: Bhavnagar (British protectorate)

name: Hyderabad State
description: Hyderabad State was an autonomous princely realm established across the Deccan plateau of south-central India by the Mughal viceroy Mir Qamar-ud-din Khan, better known as Nizam-ul-Mulk Asaf Jah I. name: Sultanate of Serdang
description: The Sultanate of Serdang was an autonomous Malay monarchy established on the eastern coast of Sumatra in modern-day North Sumatra province. Founded in 1723 following a dynastic succession dispute in the neighbouring Sultanate of Deli, the state established its capital at Perbaungan under Sultan Tuanku Umar Johan Pahlawan Alam Shah. name: Khaniadhana State

Established in 1724 by Amar Singh Judev, a Bundela Rajput prince from the royal house of Orchha, the state governed dozens of agrarian villages from the fortified town of Khaniadhana. name: Sultanate of Terengganu
description: The Sultanate of Terengganu emerged as an autonomous Malay kingdom along the north-eastern coast of the Malay Peninsula facing the South China Sea. Founded in 1725 under Sultan Zainal Abidin I, a younger brother of Sultan Abdul Jalil IV of Johor, the monarchy established its seat of power at Kuala Terengganu. name: Imamate of Futa Jallon

description: The Imamate of Futa Jallon was a theocratic Islamic state established across the central highlands of Guinea in the aftermath of a Fulani jihad launched in 1725. Ruled from the hilltop settlement of Ndu by a paramount traditional chief styled the Nkwi, the polity coordinated agricultural production, iron toolmaking and trade across the Mbaw Plain. name: Quba Khanate

name: Bahawalpur State
description: Bahawalpur State was a sovereign Muslim realm established in the southern Punjab along the banks of the Indus and Sutlej rivers by the Abbasi clan. name: Jaipur State
description: Jaipur State was a sovereign Rajput kingdom established across the north-eastern Dhundhar tract of Rajasthan by the Kachwaha dynasty. In 1727, Maharaja Sawai Jai Singh II founded the planned capital of Jaipur to replace the fortified city of Amber as the seat of royal administration. name: Greenland

name: Dewas State
description: Dewas State was an autonomous Maratha territory established on the Malwa plateau of central India by the Puar dynasty. name: Kingdom of Travancore
description: Kingdom of Travancore was a powerful sovereign state spanning the Malabar and Coromandel coastlines of southern India, established through the consolidation of the older Venad realm. name: Oguaa
description: Oguaa was a coastal Fante kingdom established along the Gulf of Guinea in modern-day southern Ghana, centred on the historic trading town of Cape Coast. name: Salyan Khanate

name: Cambay State

name: Dhar State

name: Sultanate of Lahej

name: Indore State

name: Black River Settlement
description: Black River Settlement was a British colonial logging and mercantile outpost established along the Mosquito Coast of modern Honduras. Founded in 1733 by William Pitt, the community prospered through mahogany harvesting, logwood extraction and illicit commerce with nearby Spanish captaincies. name: Jaso State

Founded in 1733 by descendants of the Orchha and Panna royal families, the small principality maintained autonomous internal governance over its agrarian estates. name: Oudh State
description: Oudh State was a prosperous autonomous realm in northern India governed by the Awadh dynasty under nominal vassalage to the Mughal Empire. name: Bantva Manavadar
description: Bantva Manavadar was an autonomous princely estate located on the Kathiawar peninsula in western Gujarat, founded by a cadet branch of the ruling Babi family of Junagadh. Established in 1734, the state exercised independent local jurisdiction over fertile agricultural villages and revenue tracts. The ruling khans maintained domestic autonomy amid shifting Maratha political currents until entering formal treaty arrangements with the British East India Company in 1819. \n\n Status: Sovereign princely state; Capital: Manavadar; Common languages: Gujarati and Urdu; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Babi; Ruler title: Khan; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1734; Succeeded by: British East India Company protectorate

name: Kurundvad State
description: Kurundvad State was a sovereign Maratha fiefdom situated along the Panchganga River in the southern Deccan plateau of modern Maharashtra. Granted in 1734 to Trimbakrao Patwardhan as a hereditary military reward by the Peshwa, the state comprised scattered enclave territories that provided revenue and soldiers for Maratha military campaigns. The ruling raos governed their domains autonomously until dividing their patrimony into separate senior and junior branches under British supervision. \n\n Status: Sovereign princely state; Capital: Kurundvad; Common languages: Marathi and Kannada; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Patwardhan; Ruler title: Rao; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1734; Preceded by: Maratha Confederacy

name: Malneta

Inhabited primarily by Khas communities, the kingdom retained political autonomy through local clan allegiances and subsistence hill agriculture. name: Porto Novo

The venture was quickly suppressed by neighbouring French and British colonial authorities, who captured the factory and ended Swedish commercial ambitions in India. \n\n Status: Colonial trading factory; Capital: Parangipettai; Common languages: Swedish and Tamil; Religion: Lutheranism; Government: Chartered company administration; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1734; Disestablished: 1 February 1734

name: Sardargarh State
description: Sardargarh State was a sovereign Muslim-ruled principality situated in the Kathiawar peninsula of modern Gujarat, founded by Sherzamankhanji Babi. As a cadet branch of the Junagadh royal line, the state governed thirteen agricultural villages and derived revenues from local cotton and grain cultivation. The ruling khans exercised independent territorial jurisdiction while navigating regional Maratha tribute demands until the British pacification of western India in the early nineteenth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign princely state; Capital: Sardargarh; Common languages: Gujarati and Urdu; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Babi; Ruler title: Khan; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1734; Succeeded by: British East India Company protectorate

name: State of the Presidi

description: State of the Presidi was a strategic coastal enclave on the southern Tuscan littoral, administered as a direct dependency of the Bourbon Kingdom of Naples. Encompassing fortified garrisons at Orbetello, Talamone, Porto Ercole and Porto Longone on Elba, the territory controlled key navigation channels throughout the Tyrrhenian Sea. name: Kingdom of Sicily

description: Durrani Empire was a powerful sovereign Afghan empire founded by Ahmad Shah Durrani of the Sadozai clan following the assassination of Nadir Shah in 1747. description: Guarded Domains of Iran was a sovereign Iranian realm established by Karim Khan Zand of the Lak ethnic group following decades of regional civil strife. From his new imperial capital at Shiraz, Karim Khan rebuilt urban markets, fostered oceanic and overland trade and restored civic peace across central and southern Iran, modestly adopting the title of deputy of the people. Frequently influenced by the more powerful neighbouring Quba and Shirvan khanates, Salyan retained domestic administrative self-rule until being formally absorbed into the Shirvan Khanate in 1790. \n\n Status: Vassal khanate under Persian suzerainty; Capital: Salyan; Common languages: Azerbaijani and Persian; Religion: Shia Islam; Government: Hereditary khanate; Ruler title: Khan; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1749; Disestablished: 1790; Succeeded by: Shirvan Khanate

Centred upon the fortified walled town of Gumel, the state developed extensive cereal farming and livestock trade while maintaining a disciplined cavalry force to repel raids from Bornu and Damagaram. The sultans maintained traditional clan justice, regulated maritime livestock and frankincense commerce, and defended pastoral grazing boundaries until signing protectorate treaties establishing British Somaliland in the 1880s. \n\n Status: Sovereign sultanate; Capital: Hargeisa; Common languages: Somali and Arabic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Traditional monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Guled; Ruler title: Sultan; Historical era: Pre-colonial Africa; Established: 1 August 1750; Disestablished: 1885; Succeeded by: British Somaliland

name: Bandounga

name: Beri State

name: Buea

name: Fisakana Kingdom

name: Kingdom of Bafut

name: Kothi State

name: Lalangina Kingdom

name: Landuma

name: Makran State

name: Nikki
