description: Tawngpeng State was a mountainous Shan principality situated in the highlands of the Northern Shan States in eastern Burma. Inhabited predominantly by the Palaung people, the realm was governed by hereditary rulers from their capital at Namhsan and held a lucrative monopoly over regional tea cultivation. The state was a loyal tributary vassal to the Konbaung court of Burma, providing annual tribute and military levies until British imperial forces annexed the region in 1886. \n\n Status: Vassal state of the Konbaung dynasty; Capital: Namhsan; Common languages: Palaung, Shan and Burmese; Religion: Theravada Buddhism; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Ruler title: Sawbwa; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1754; Disestablished: 1886; Succeeded by: British Burma

name: Duchy of Pakualaman
description: The Duchy of Pakualaman was a hereditary Javanese princely domain created in south-central Java as an autonomous enclave within the Sultanate of Yogyakarta. Established under Dutch colonial oversight as a counterpart to Mangkunegaran in Surakarta, the court was ruled by Prince Paku Alam from his palace complex at Pakualaman. The duchy maintained a small military corps and sustained refined Javanese courtly traditions under Dutch East Indies supervision until the Japanese invasion of Java in March 1942. \n\n Status: Dutch protectorate; Capital: Pakualaman; Common languages: Javanese and Dutch; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Hereditary constitutional principality; Ruling dynasty: House of Pakualaman; Ruler title: Duke of Pakualaman; Historical era: Modern period; Established: 13 February 1755; Disestablished: 10 March 1942; Succeeded by: Japanese Empire (Military Administration)

name: Principality of Mangkunegaran
description: The Principality of Mangkunegaran was an autonomous Javanese royal domain formed following the division of the Mataram realm and formalised by the 1757 Treaty of Salatiga. Governed by the hereditary Prince Mangkunegara from his royal palace in Surakarta, the principality functioned as a semi-independent protectorate under the Dutch East India Company and the Netherlands colonial government. The court fostered classical literature, traditional dance and its renowned Mangkunegaran Legion until the Japanese occupation in March 1942. \n\n Status: Dutch protectorate; Capital: Mangkunagaran; Common languages: Javanese and Dutch; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Princely monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Mangkunegaran; Ruler title: Prince Mangkunegara; Historical era: Modern period; Established: 13 February 1755; Disestablished: 10 March 1942; Succeeded by: Japanese Empire (Military Administration)

name: Surakarta Sunanate
description: The Surakarta Sunanate was a major Javanese monarchy created following the partition of the Mataram Sultanate under the 1755 Treaty of Giyanti. Ruled by the Susuhunan from the Kraton of Surakarta in central Java, the state was placed under Dutch colonial suzerainty while retaining substantial domestic autonomy and cultural primacy. The sunanate survived the colonial era and the Pacific War before its direct administrative powers were dissolved upon the establishment of the Republic of Indonesia in August 1945. \n\n Status: Dutch protectorate; Capital: Surakarta; Common languages: Javanese and Dutch; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Absolute monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Mataram dynasty; Ruler title: Susuhunan; Historical era: Modern period; Established: 13 February 1755; Disestablished: 17 August 1945; Succeeded by: Republic of Indonesia

name: Yogyakarta Sultanate
description: The Yogyakarta Sultanate was a sovereign Javanese realm established by Sultan Hamengkubuwono I following the partition of the Mataram Empire under the Treaty of Giyanti. Governed from the Kraton of Yogyakarta in south-central Java, the sultanate maintained rich cultural traditions and resisted European encroachments despite operating under Dutch colonial protection. The realm retained considerable administrative authority until Dutch colonial governance collapsed during the Japanese invasion of Indonesia in March 1942. \n\n Status: Dutch protectorate; Capital: Yogyakarta; Common languages: Javanese and Dutch; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Absolute monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Hamengkubuwono; Ruler title: Sultan; Historical era: Modern period; Established: 13 February 1755; Disestablished: 10 March 1942; Succeeded by: Japanese Empire (Military Administration)

name: Kingdom of Burma (Military Occupation)
description: The Kingdom of Burma (Military Occupation) comprised the southern territories of Lower Burma temporarily garrisoned and governed by the advancing armed forces of King Alaungpaya. Established during the Konbaung offensive against the Restored Hanthawaddy Kingdom, this martial operational zone spanned key river corridors along the Irrawaddy Delta and surrounding Mon homelands. Military officers administered captured towns under martial discipline until the decisive capture and destruction of Pegu in May 1757 consolidated Konbaung imperial rule. \n\n Status: Military occupation zone; Capital: None (decentralised); Common languages: Burmese and Mon; Religion: Theravada Buddhism; Government: Military administrative zone; Head of state: King Alaungpaya; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 5 April 1755; Disestablished: 6 May 1757; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Burma

name: Corsican Republic
description: The Corsican Republic was a sovereign constitutional state established on the Mediterranean island of Corsica after Pasquale Paoli led a successful uprising against the Republic of Genoa. Paoli promulgated Europe's first modern democratic constitution, introducing representative parliamentary government, female suffrage and an indigenous judicial system centred at Corte. The fledgling republic maintained its independence until 1769, when French expeditionary forces conquered the island at the Battle of Ponte Novu. \n\n Status: Sovereign constitutional republic; Capital: Corte; Official languages: Italian; Common languages: Corsican; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Constitutional republic; Ruler title: General of the Nation; Head of state: Pasquale Paoli; Historical era: Age of Enlightenment; Established: 1 December 1755; Disestablished: 9 May 1769; Succeeded by: Kingdom of France

name: Kingdom of Kom
description: The Kingdom of Kom was a precolonial monarchical state situated in the mountainous Bamenda Grassfields of northwestern Cameroon. Established by the Kom people, the kingdom was governed by a sacred monarch titled the Fon, who ruled alongside the powerful Quifon traditional council from the mountaintop capital of Laikom. The realm maintained economic vitality and regional military influence until German imperial forces incorporated the Grassfields chiefdoms into German Kamerun in 1901. \n\n Status: Precolonial kingdom; Capital: Laikom; Common languages: Kom; Religion: Traditional animism; Government: Traditional monarchy; Ruler title: Fon; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1756; Disestablished: 1901; Succeeded by: German Kamerun

name: Seychelles
description: Seychelles was an insular French colonial possession encompassing the granitic and coralline archipelago of the western Indian Ocean. Formally claimed for the French Crown in 1756 by Captain Nicholas Morphey, the territory was administered from Isle de France and settled primarily by French planters and enslaved Africans who developed spice and coconut estates. The islands functioned as an overseas naval and agricultural outpost until British naval forces captured the colony in May 1794. \n\n Status: Colony of the Kingdom of France; Capital: Victoria; Common languages: French and Seychellois Creole; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Colonial administration; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1757; Disestablished: 17 May 1794; Succeeded by: Seychelles (British colony)

name: Alipura State
description: Alipura State was an autonomous princely realm located in the Bundelkhand region of modern-day Madhya Pradesh in central India. Founded in 1757 by the Bundela Rajput leader Aman Singh, the state was administered from the fortified township of Alipura. The small principality retained its local self-governance amid frequent Maratha and Mughal incursions until concluding a treaty of British protection in 1809, briefly regaining independence after Indian partition before integrating into India in 1950. \n\n Status: Princely state; Capital: Alipura; Common languages: Hindi and Bundeli; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Princely monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Bundela; Ruler title: Rao; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1758; Disestablished: 1950; Succeeded by: Republic of India

name: Hsawnghsup State
label: shan states
description: Hsawnghsup State was an outlying Shan principality situated in the upper Chindwin River valley and the neighbouring Kabaw Valley near the border with Manipur. Governed by hereditary Shan sawbwas from the riverine settlement of Thaungdut, the state paid formal tribute to the Konbaung monarchs of Burma. The principality preserved its local institutions and guarded the western marches until British imperial forces annexed Upper Burma and established colonial administration in 1886. \n\n Status: Vassal state of the Konbaung dynasty; Capital: Hsawnghsup; Common languages: Shan, Manipuri and Burmese; Religion: Theravada Buddhism; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Ruler title: Sawbwa; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1758; Disestablished: 1886; Succeeded by: British Burma

name: Pashalik of Scutari
description: The Pashalik of Scutari was an autonomous, de facto independent Ottoman province ruled by the Albanian Bushati family from their fortress city of Shkodër. Under dynamic leaders such as Kara Mahmud Bushati, the pashalik expanded across modern northern Albania, Montenegro, Kosovo and western Macedonia, maintaining diplomatic ties with European courts. The family held extensive autonomy until Ottoman imperial armies defeated Mustafa Pasha Bushati in 1831–1832, restoring direct central administration. \n\n Status: Autonomous pashalik of the Ottoman Empire; Capital: Shkodër; Common languages: Albanian, Ottoman Turkish and Serbian; Religion: Sunni Islam, Roman Catholicism and Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Hereditary pashalik; Ruling dynasty: Bushati dynasty; Ruler title: Pasha; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1758; Disestablished: 1832; Succeeded by: Ottoman Empire

name: Balasinor State
description: Balasinor State was an autonomous princely domain established in the plains of eastern Gujarat, western India. Founded in September 1758 by Sardar Muhammad Khan Babi, an influential Pashtun commander whose family had governed under the late Mughal Empire, the state had its capital at Balasinor. The nawabs defended their sovereign rights against surrounding Maratha and Gaekwad expansion before placing the state under British East India Company protection in the mid-nineteenth century. \n\n Status: Princely state; Capital: Balasinor; Common languages: Gujarati, Urdu and Persian; Religion: Sunni Islam and Hinduism; Government: Princely monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Babi dynasty; Ruler title: Nawab; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 28 September 1758; Disestablished: 1851; Succeeded by: Balasinor State (British protectorate)

name: Bade Emirate
description: The Bade Emirate was an independent traditional state located in the semi-arid Yobe River basin of northeastern Nigeria. Inhabited by the Bade people, the emirate was ruled by a hereditary monarch titled the Mai Bade from his fortified headquarters at Gashua. The state fiercely resisted absorption by both the Kanem-Bornu Empire and the Fulani jihad of the Sokoto Caliphate until British imperial expeditions subjugated northern Nigeria in 1903. \n\n Status: Traditional emirate; Capital: Gashua; Common languages: Bade, Kanuri and Hausa; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Traditional monarchy; Ruler title: Mai Bade; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1760; Disestablished: 1903; Succeeded by: Northern Nigeria Protectorate

name: Kingdom of Mambo a Chidima
description: The Kingdom of Mambo a Chidima was an autonomous Shona rump state that carried forward the dynastic heritage of the historic Mutapa Empire in northern Mozambique. Centred in the rugged Chidima highlands south of the Zambezi River, the state was ruled by traditional monarchs bearing the imperial title of Mwenemutapa. The kingdom maintained indigenous customs and resisted Portuguese colonial encroachment for more than a century until Portuguese military forces extinguished the dynasty in 1918. \n\n Status: Traditional kingdom; Capital: Chidima; Common languages: Shona; Religion: Traditional Shona beliefs; Government: Traditional monarchy; Ruler title: Mwenemutapa; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1760; Disestablished: 1918; Succeeded by: Portuguese East Africa

name: Marie-Galante
description: Marie-Galante was a circular island colony in the Lesser Antilles of the Caribbean Sea that fell under British military and colonial administration during several wartime occupations. Known for its productive sugarcane plantations worked by enslaved Africans, the island was governed from Grand-Bourg as a tactical naval prize. British authority was repeatedly contested by France until the final conclusion of the Napoleonic Wars in 1815 returned the dependency permanently to French Guadeloupe. \n\n Status: Colony of Great Britain; Capital: Grand-Bourg; Official languages: English; Common languages: French and Antillean Creole; Religion: Roman Catholicism and Anglicanism; Government: Colonial administration; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1760; Disestablished: 1816; Succeeded by: Guadeloupe (French colony)

name: Principality of Torriglia
label: holy roman empire
description: The Principality of Torriglia was an imperial fief of the Holy Roman Empire nestled in the Ligurian Apennines northeast of Genoa. Ruled by the illustrious Doria-Pamphili-Landi family, the territory was elevated from a marquisate to a sovereign principality by Emperor Francis I in May 1760. The princes maintained administrative autonomy and minting privileges from Torriglia Castle until revolutionary French forces reorganised northern Italy, dissolving the fief into the Ligurian Republic in August 1797. \n\n Status: Imperial principality of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Torriglia; Common languages: Ligurian and Italian; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal principality; Ruling dynasty: Doria-Pamphili-Landi; Ruler title: Prince; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 13 May 1760; Disestablished: 6 August 1797; Succeeded by: Ligurian Republic

name: Bali-Kumbat
description: Bali-Kumbat was a sovereign precolonial kingdom situated in the fertile Ndop plain of the Western Grassfields in Cameroon. Established by migrating Chamba warrior clans in the late eighteenth century, the state was governed by a sacred traditional monarch known as the Fon. The kingdom maintained extensive agricultural settlements, defensive fortifications and trading ties throughout the region until German imperial forces occupied the Bamenda Grassfields in 1901. \n\n Status: Precolonial kingdom; Capital: Bali-Kumbat; Common languages: Mubako and Chamba; Religion: Traditional animism; Government: Traditional monarchy; Ruler title: Fon; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1761; Disestablished: 1901; Succeeded by: German Kamerun

name: Bali-Nyonga
description: Bali-Nyonga was a prominent precolonial chiefdom established in the North West Region of Cameroon by Chamba Leko migrants who settled in the Grassfields. Governed by a traditional ruler titled the Fon from the settlement of Bali-Nyonga, the kingdom developed a powerful military apparatus and adopted the Mungaka language. The polity commanded regional commerce and dominated surrounding chiefdoms until concluding treaties that brought it under German imperial colonial control in 1901. \n\n Status: Precolonial kingdom; Capital: Bali-Nyonga; Common languages: Mungaka; Religion: Traditional animism; Government: Traditional monarchy; Ruler title: Fon; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1761; Disestablished: 1901; Succeeded by: German Kamerun

name: Bora Bora
description: Bora Bora was an independent Polynesian kingdom centred on the volcanic island of Bora Bora and surrounding atolls in the Leeward Society Islands. Governed by hereditary paramount chiefs known as ari'i from their administrative settlement at Vaitape, the realm maintained a formidable maritime reputation across the South Pacific. The island remained politically autonomous until nineteenth-century Christian missions and expanding French colonial claims culminated in the annexation of the Leeward Islands by France. \n\n Status: Sovereign island kingdom; Capital: Vaitape; Common languages: Tahitian; Religion: Traditional Polynesian religion; Government: Traditional monarchy; Ruler title: Ari'i; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1761; Disestablished: 1848; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Bora Bora (French protectorate)

name: Kalsia State
description: Kalsia State was an autonomous Sikh principality established in the Cis-Sutlej region of the eastern Punjab by Sardar Gurbaksh Singh Kalsia. Deriving from the Karor Singhia misl, the state was ruled from Chhachhrauli and encompassed productive agricultural tracts across modern Haryana and Punjab. The ruling Jat Sikh dynasty defended their sovereignty against neighbouring Afghan and Maratha invaders before placing the principality under British protection in the early nineteenth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign princely state; Capital: Chhachhrauli; Common languages: Punjabi and Hindustani; Religion: Sikhism, Hinduism and Islam; Government: Princely monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Kalsia dynasty; Ruler title: Sardar; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1761; Disestablished: 1802; Succeeded by: Kalsia State (British protectorate)

name: Kirua
label: african great lakes kingdoms
description: Kirua was an autonomous Chagga kingdom located on the fertile southern volcanic slopes of Mount Kilimanjaro in modern northeastern Tanzania. Governed by hereditary monarchs titled the Mangi from Kirua Vunjo, the state prospered through intensive banana cultivation, terraced agriculture and participation in regional caravan trade. The chiefdom maintained its internal independence amidst rivalries with neighbouring Chagga realms until the German East Africa Company imposed colonial rule in 1891. \n\n Status: Traditional kingdom; Capital: Kirua Vunjo; Common languages: Kichagga and Swahili; Religion: Traditional Chagga religion; Government: Traditional monarchy; Ruler title: Mangi; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1761; Disestablished: 1891; Succeeded by: German East Africa

name: Samthar State
description: Samthar State was an independent princely realm established in the plains of Bundelkhand across the modern borderlands of Uttar Pradesh and Madhya Pradesh. Founded in 1760 by Ranjit Singh of the Bargujar Rajput clan during the dislocation caused by Maratha campaigns, the state was administered from the imposing stronghold of Samthar Fort. The rulers asserted complete autonomy from Datia until negotiating a treaty of subsidiary alliance with the British East India Company in 1818. \n\n Status: Sovereign princely state; Capital: Samthar; Common languages: Bundeli and Hindi; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Princely monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Bargujar Rajput; Ruler title: Raja; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1761; Disestablished: 1818; Succeeded by: Samthar State (British protectorate)

name: Wollo
description: Wollo was an autonomous highland kingdom established in the central Ethiopian plateau across the historic province of Bete Amhara. Governed by the Muslim Warra Himano dynasty from their royal courts in the Wollo mountains, the realm emerged as a decisive military and political force during the Era of the Princes. The rulers exercised extensive influence over the imperial throne in Gondar until Emperor Menelik II subdued the region and re-established centralised Ethiopian imperial governance in 1897. \n\n Status: Autonomous kingdom; Capital: Walo; Common languages: Amharic and Oromo; Religion: Sunni Islam and Ethiopian Orthodox Christianity; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Warra Himano; Ruler title: Ras; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1761; Disestablished: 1897; Succeeded by: Ethiopian Empire

name: Mughal Empire
description: The Mughal Empire during this phase existed as a protected imperial realm in northern India under the suzerainty of the Durrani Empire of Afghanistan. Following the Third Battle of Panipat, the Afghan monarch Ahmad Shah Durrani recognised Shah Alam II as emperor while installing Afghan-aligned regents to oversee imperial administration in Delhi. The beleaguered court maintained titular sovereignty over a shrunken domain until Maratha confederate forces recaptured Delhi in 1772 and restored imperial autonomy. \n\n Status: Protectorate under the Durrani Empire; Capital: Delhi; Official languages: Persian; Common languages: Urdu and Hindustani; Religion: Sunni Islam and Hinduism; Government: Absolute monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Mughal dynasty; Ruler title: Emperor; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1762; Disestablished: 1772; Succeeded by: Mughal Empire (Maratha protectorate)

name: Russian-American Company
description: The Russian-American Company was a state-chartered colonial trading monopoly established by the Russian Empire to govern Russian America and manage maritime commerce across the North Pacific. Operating primarily from settlements at Kodiak and later Sitka, the company directed commercial sea otter fur harvests, constructed shipyards and established trading posts extending to northern California. The enterprise exercised administrative and civil authority over colonial settlements and indigenous populations until the sale of Alaska to the United States in 1867. \n\n Status: Chartered colonial company rule; Capital: Kodiak and Sitka; Official languages: Russian; Common languages: Russian, Aleut and Tlingit; Religion: Russian Orthodoxy; Government: Chartered corporation; Head of state: Emperor of Russia; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1762; Disestablished: 18 October 1867; Succeeded by: Department of Alaska

name: Duchy of Holstein-Gottorp
label: holy roman empire
description: The Duchy of Holstein-Gottorp during this interval functioned as a territorial possession of the Russian Empire within the Holy Roman Empire. When Duke Charles Peter Ulrich ascended the Russian imperial throne as Tsar Peter III in January 1762, his ancestral patrimony in Ducal Holstein entered personal union with the imperial crown. Governed from the Baltic port of Kiel, the territory remained under Russian ducal administration until Catherine the Great ceded the Gottorp lands to Denmark through the 1773 Treaty of Tsarskoye Selo. \n\n Status: Imperial possession of the Russian Empire; Capital: Kiel; Official languages: German; Common languages: Low German and Danish; Religion: Lutheranism; Government: Feudal duchy in personal union; Ruling dynasty: House of Holstein-Gottorp; Ruler title: Duke; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 5 January 1762; Disestablished: 1 June 1773; Succeeded by: Duchy of Holstein

name: Kingdom of Kartli-Kakheti
description: The Kingdom of Kartli-Kakheti was an independent eastern Georgian state established through the formal unification of the historic kingdoms of Kartli and Kakheti under King Heraclius II. Ruling from the capital at Tbilisi, Heraclius modernised his army, fostered artisan crafts and asserted regional dominance across the South Caucasus following the retreat of Iranian suzerainty. The sovereign kingdom preserved its independence against Ottoman and Persian threats until concluding the Treaty of Georgievsk with imperial Russia in July 1783. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Tbilisi; Official languages: Georgian; Religion: Georgian Orthodox Christianity; Government: Absolute monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Bagrationi dynasty; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 8 January 1762; Disestablished: 24 July 1783; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Kartli-Kakheti (Russian protectorate)

name: Colony of Saint Vincent
description: The Colony of Saint Vincent was an insular British possession in the southeastern Caribbean acquired from France under the terms of the 1763 Treaty of Paris. Governed from the coastal port of Kingstown, the island became a major producer of sugar and arrowroot cultivated by enslaved African labourers. Colonial authorities faced sustained resistance from the indigenous and Black Carib populations during the Carib Wars before establishing firm plantation governance that endured until full independence in 1979. \n\n Status: Crown colony; Capital: Kingstown; Official languages: English; Common languages: Vincentian Creole; Religion: Anglicanism and Roman Catholicism; Government: Colonial administration; Head of state: Monarch of Great Britain; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 10 February 1763; Disestablished: 27 October 1979; Succeeded by: Saint Vincent and the Grenadines

name: Colony of Saint-Pierre and Miquelon
description: The Colony of Saint-Pierre and Miquelon was a French overseas archipelago located in the northwestern Atlantic Ocean off the southern coast of Newfoundland. Retained by France under the 1763 Treaty of Paris following the loss of New France, the islands served as a vital base and seasonal harbour for the French Grand Banks cod fishing fleet. Administered from Saint-Pierre, the colony survived several British wartime seizures and expulsions before returning definitively to French colonial governance in 1816. \n\n Status: Colony of the Kingdom of France; Capital: Saint-Pierre; Official languages: French; Common languages: French and Basque; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Colonial administration; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 10 February 1763; Disestablished: 27 October 1946; Succeeded by: Saint-Pierre and Miquelon (Overseas territory)

name: Dominica
description: Dominica was a British island colony in the Lesser Antilles of the eastern Caribbean, ceded by the Kingdom of France following the conclusion of the Seven Years' War in 1763. Governed from the western coastal settlement of Roseau, the island developed a plantation economy centred on coffee, cocoa and sugar cultivation worked by enslaved Africans. British administrators encountered persistent challenges from the island's mountainous terrain and indigenous Kalinago settlements, maintaining imperial rule until the nation achieved independence in 1978. \n\n Status: Crown colony; Capital: Roseau; Official languages: English; Common languages: Dominican Creole French; Religion: Roman Catholicism and Anglicanism; Government: Colonial administration; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 10 February 1763; Disestablished: 11 March 1978; Succeeded by: Commonwealth of Dominica

name: Grenada
description: Grenada was an insular British colony located in the southern Caribbean, transferred from French control to Great Britain under the 1763 Treaty of Paris. Administered from the deep-water harbour town of St. George's, the territory expanded into a thriving agricultural hub renowned for the export of sugarcane, cocoa and nutmeg. The colony weathered political instability during the pro-French Fédon rebellion of 1795 before undergoing institutional modernisation that paved the way for self-governance and full independence. \n\n Status: Crown colony; Capital: St. George's; Official languages: English; Common languages: Grenadian Creole English and Grenadian Creole French; Religion: Roman Catholicism and Anglicanism; Government: Colonial administration; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 10 February 1763; Disestablished: 3 March 1967; Succeeded by: Associated State of Grenada

name: Province of East Florida
label: thirteen colonies
description: The Province of East Florida was a British crown colony created from the eastern portion of Spanish Florida following the 1763 Treaty of Paris. Governed from the historic fortified town of St. Augustine, the province attracted Loyalist planters and merchants who established indigo, timber and citrus enterprises along the St. Johns River. East Florida remained resolutely loyal to the British Crown throughout the American Revolutionary War before being retroceded to Spain under the Treaty of Versailles in 1783. \n\n Status: Crown colony; Capital: St. Augustine; Official languages: English; Common languages: English and Spanish; Religion: Anglicanism and Roman Catholicism; Government: Colonial administration; Ruler title: Governor; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 10 February 1763; Disestablished: 20 January 1783; Succeeded by: Spanish Florida

name: Province of West Florida
label: thirteen colonies
description: The Province of West Florida was an expansive British North American colony established in 1763 from former French Louisiana and western Spanish Florida between the Apalachicola and Mississippi rivers. Headquartered at the Gulf Coast port of Pensacola, the colony developed vibrant timber and fur trades and maintained key defensive garrisons along the lower Mississippi. West Florida declined to join the American Revolution and provided safe haven for southern Loyalists until Spanish forces under Bernardo de Gálvez conquered Pensacola in 1781. \n\n Status: Crown colony; Capital: Pensacola; Official languages: English; Common languages: English, French and Spanish; Religion: Anglicanism; Government: Colonial administration; Ruler title: Governor; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 10 February 1763; Disestablished: 20 January 1783; Succeeded by: Spanish West Florida

name: Pontiac's Rebels
description: Pontiac's Rebels comprised an autonomous multi-tribal Native American warrior confederacy formed across the Great Lakes and Ohio Country in 1763. Mobilised by the Odawa chief Pontiac alongside Ojibwe, Potawatomi, Wyandot, Shawnee and Delaware leaders, the coalition sought to expel British military garrisons following the French and Indian War. The confederacy captured nine British frontier forts and besieged Detroit and Fort Pitt before negotiations resulted in modified imperial trade policies and the Royal Proclamation of 1763. \n\n Status: Pan-tribal resistance confederacy; Capital: None (decentralised); Common languages: Odawa, Ojibwe, Potawatomi, Wyandot and Delaware; Religion: Traditional indigenous beliefs; Government: Military tribal alliance; Head of state: Pontiac; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 16 May 1763; Disestablished: 1765; Succeeded by: British North America

name: Jind State
description: Jind State was an independent Sikh principality located in the Cis-Sutlej region of the eastern Punjab, founded in 1763 by Raja Gajpat Singh of the Phulkian Sidhu Jat clan. Operating from the fortified settlements of Jind and Sangrur, the dynasty consolidated control over fertile agrarian tracts following the collapse of Mughal imperial authority in Delhi. The state repelled neighbouring Afghan and Maratha armies before concluding formal protective treaties with the British East India Company in the early nineteenth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign princely state; Capital: Sangrur; Common languages: Punjabi and Hindustani; Religion: Sikhism and Hinduism; Government: Princely monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Phulkian dynasty; Ruler title: Raja; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1764; Disestablished: 1802; Succeeded by: Jind State (British protectorate)

name: Nabha State
description: Nabha State was an autonomous Sikh principality established in the Cis-Sutlej plains of the Punjab by Raja Hamir Singh, a prominent chieftain of the Phulkian misl. Governed from the fortified city of Nabha, the state derived significant revenues from rich agricultural estates and maintained a well-equipped army of cavalrymen and foot soldiers. The rulers preserved their territorial sovereignty amid regional turmoil caused by Maratha and Afghan incursions until entering British protection in 1809. \n\n Status: Sovereign princely state; Capital: Nabha; Common languages: Punjabi and Hindustani; Religion: Sikhism and Hinduism; Government: Princely monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Phulkian dynasty; Ruler title: Raja; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1764; Disestablished: 1802; Succeeded by: Nabha State (British protectorate)

name: Kingdom of Poland and the Grand Duchy of Lithuania
description: The Kingdom of Poland and the Grand Duchy of Lithuania during this period existed as a client protectorate dominated by the Russian Empire following the election of King Stanisław August Poniatowski in 1764. Governed from Warsaw under the oversight of Russian ambassadors and occupying imperial garrisons, the Commonwealth experienced severe political paralysis under the aristocratic liberum veto. Armed nationalist resistance by the Bar Confederation provoked the First Partition of Poland in 1772, ultimately leading to total territorial dismemberment by 1795. \n\n Status: Russian protectorate; Capital: Warsaw; Official languages: Polish and Latin; Common languages: Polish, Ruthenian and Lithuanian; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Elective monarchy and noble democracy; Ruler title: King of Poland and Grand Duke of Lithuania; Head of state: Stanisław August Poniatowski; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 7 September 1764; Disestablished: 24 October 1795; Succeeded by: Russian Empire, Kingdom of Prussia and Habsburg Monarchy

name: Falkland Islands
description: The Falkland Islands under French rule constituted a strategic South Atlantic naval outpost established in 1764 by explorer Louis-Antoine de Bougainville at Port Louis on East Falkland. Named the Îles Malouines after the port of Saint-Malo, the settlement was created to secure French navigational routes around Cape Horn and support overseas whaling and maritime trade. Following formal diplomatic protests by the Spanish Crown regarding territorial claims, France peacefully transferred sovereignty and administrative control of the colony to Spain in 1767. \n\n Status: Colony of the Kingdom of France; Capital: Port Louis; Official languages: French; Common languages: French; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Colonial administration; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1765; Disestablished: 1767; Succeeded by: Puerto Soledad (Spanish Empire)

name: Sawantwadi State
label: indian princely states
description: Sawantwadi State was a Maratha princely domain situated along the Konkan coastal plain between Portuguese Goa and the Western Ghats in western India. Ruled by the Sawant Bhonsle dynasty from their palace at Sawantwadi, the state commanded defensive hill forts and developed maritime forces that contested coastal waters with European trading companies. The principality entered treaty relations with the British East India Company in 1765 and endured as a recognised princely state until merging into the Indian Union in 1948. \n\n Status: Princely state under British paramountcy; Capital: Sawantwadi; Common languages: Marathi and Malvani; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Princely monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Sawant Bhonsle; Ruler title: Raja Bahadur; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 4 July 1765; Disestablished: 15 August 1947; Succeeded by: Republic of India

name: Cooch Behar State
label: indian princely states
description: Cooch Behar State was a prominent northeastern Indian princely realm situated on the alluvial plains south of the Himalayan kingdom of Bhutan. Formed from the western remnants of the Kamata Kingdom under the Koch dynasty, the state had its capital at Cooch Behar. Facing persistent Bhutanese military invasions, the royal court concluded a treaty of subsidiary protection with the British East India Company in 1773, safeguarding its autonomy until acceding to India in 1949. \n\n Status: Princely state under British paramountcy; Capital: Cooch Behar; Common languages: Bengali and Kamtapuri; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Princely monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Koch dynasty; Ruler title: Maharaja; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 8 December 1765; Disestablished: 1950; Succeeded by: Republic of India

name: Ajaigarh State
description: Ajaigarh State was an autonomous Bundela Rajput principality established in the rugged Bundelkhand region of central India by Raja Guman Singh. Centred on the formidable hilltop citadel of Ajaigarh, the ruler asserted sovereign control over surrounding forested districts during the political decentralisation following the decline of Mughal authority. The state maintained independent defence forces against regional Maratha raiding parties until concluding a treaty of British protection in 1810. \n\n Status: Sovereign princely state; Capital: Ajaigarh; Common languages: Bundeli and Hindi; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Princely monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Bundela; Ruler title: Sawai Maharaja; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1766; Disestablished: 1810; Succeeded by: Ajaigarh State (British protectorate)

name: Bijawar State
description: Bijawar State was an independent princely realm situated in the Bundelkhand Agency of central India, founded in 1765 by Bir Singh Deo, a scion of the Bundela Rajput lineage. Governed from the settlement of Bijawar, the principality encompassed extensive teak forests, fertile valleys and mineral reserves across the modern Chhatarpur district. The state preserved local sovereignty through diplomatic alliances and military vigilance until entering a subsidiary relationship with the British Crown in 1801. \n\n Status: Sovereign princely state; Capital: Bijawar; Common languages: Bundeli and Hindi; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Princely monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Bundela; Ruler title: Maharaja; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1766; Disestablished: 1801; Succeeded by: Bijawar State (British protectorate)

name: Charkhari State
description: Charkhari State was an autonomous princely realm in northern India founded in 1765 by Khuman Singh, a Bundela Rajput prince who broke away from the Panna kingdom. Administered from the fortified lakeside town of Charkhari in modern Uttar Pradesh, the state maintained defensive outposts and generated revenues from agrarian estates. The principality preserved its political independence during the protracted Maratha wars before concluding a formal treaty of protection with Great Britain in 1804. \n\n Status: Sovereign princely state; Capital: Charkhari; Common languages: Bundeli and Hindi; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Princely monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Bundela; Ruler title: Maharaja; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1766; Disestablished: 1802; Succeeded by: Charkhari State (British protectorate)

name: Great Qing (Military Occupation)
description: Great Qing (Military Occupation) comprised the provisional martial territories and frontier operational commands governed by the Eight Banners and Green Standard armies during foreign campaigns in Burma, northern Vietnam and Taiwan. Operating under imperial field commanders, these military occupational zones lacked a fixed civilian capital and imposed martial administration over occupied border passes and fortified garrisons. Military officers managed supply requisitions and local policing until diplomatic settlements or strategic troop withdrawals returned territories to civil authority. \n\n Status: Military occupation zone; Capital: None (decentralised); Official languages: Manchu and Mandarin; Religion: Traditional Chinese religions and Buddhism; Government: Military administrative zone; Head of state: Qianlong Emperor; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1766; Disestablished: 9 June 1885; Succeeded by: Great Qing

name: Kingdom of Luang Phrabang
description: The Kingdom of Luang Phrabang during this era was a tributary Lao kingdom located along the upper Mekong River in modern northern Laos. Governed from the ancient royal city of Luang Phrabang by King Surinyavong II, the realm emerged from the 1707 partition of Lan Xang but was compelled to acknowledge the suzerainty of the Burmese Konbaung dynasty. The monarchy provided tribute and military manpower to Burmese armies until Siamese forces invaded northern Laos in 1779 and reasserted Siamese dominance. \n\n Status: Tributary vassal state under Burma; Capital: Luang Phrabang; Common languages: Lao; Religion: Theravada Buddhism; Government: Absolute monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Luang Phrabang dynasty; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1766; Disestablished: 1779; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Luang Phrabang (Siamese vassal)

name: Kingdom of Vientiane
description: The Kingdom of Vientiane was a Lao monarchical realm centred in the middle Mekong River basin that operated as a tributary vassal of the Burmese Konbaung dynasty. Governed from the capital city of Vientiane by King Ong Long and King Bunsan, the court aligned with Burma to counter military pressure from neighbouring Luang Phrabang and the Siamese kingdom of Ayutthaya. The kingdom remained under Burmese tributary influence until a Siamese invasion in 1779 captured Vientiane and reduced it to a Siamese vassal. \n\n Status: Tributary vassal state under Burma; Capital: Vientiane; Common languages: Lao; Religion: Theravada Buddhism; Government: Absolute monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Vientiane dynasty; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1766; Disestablished: 1825; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Vientiane (Siamese vassal)

name: Khalifa Domain
description: The Khalifa Domain was an independent maritime principality founded by the Al Khalifa branch of the Bani Utbah tribal confederation along the coast of eastern Arabia. Headquartered at the fortified trading and pearl-fishing port of Zubarah on the northwestern shore of the Qatar peninsula, the dynasty dominated Persian Gulf shipping routes and pearling banks. The rulers expanded across the Gulf to conquer Bahrain in 1783, preserving sovereign autonomy until concluding protective agreements with Great Britain in the early twentieth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign maritime sheikhdom; Capital: Zubarah; Common languages: Arabic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Traditional sheikhdom; Ruling dynasty: House of Khalifa; Ruler title: Sheikh; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1767; Disestablished: 3 November 1916; Succeeded by: Sheikhdom of Qatar (British protectorate)

name: Port Egmont
description: Port Egmont was a fortified British naval station and garrison established on Saunders Island off the northwestern coast of West Falkland. Founded in 1765 by Commodore John Byron and developed by Captain John MacBride, the outpost asserted British sovereignty over the South Atlantic archipelago and served as an oceanic replenishment base. The settlement sparked a major international confrontation when a Spanish fleet expelled the garrison in 1770, but Britain reoccupied the station in 1771 before voluntarily evacuating it in 1774. \n\n Status: Naval outpost and settlement; Capital: None (decentralised); Official languages: English; Religion: Anglicanism; Government: Naval colonial garrison; Ruler title: Naval Officer in Command; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1767; Disestablished: 1775; Succeeded by: British Overseas Territories

name: Maratha Empire (Military Occupation)
description: The Maratha Empire (Military Occupation) encompassed temporary martial operational zones established by the confederate armies of the Peshwa and regional Maratha sardars across southern and central India. Deployed during campaigns against the Kingdom of Mysore, the Nizam of Hyderabad and coastal rulers, these occupational zones lacked a fixed capital and were administered directly by field generals. Maratha military governors collected chauth, garrisoned captured hill forts and secured logistical corridors until formal peace treaties restored civilian administration. \n\n Status: Military occupation zone; Capital: None (decentralised); Common languages: Marathi; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Military administrative command; Ruler title: Peshwa; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1 February 1767; Disestablished: 18 March 1792; Succeeded by: Maratha Empire

name: Hyderabad State (Military Occupation)
description: Hyderabad State (Military Occupation) comprised the operational martial territories garrisoned by the armed forces of the Nizam of Hyderabad in the Deccan plateau. Maintained during allied campaigns against the Kingdom of Mysore alongside the Marathas and the British East India Company, these command sectors were governed by Nizamite commanders under strict martial jurisdiction. The military administration supervised the requisition of grain, managed strategic outposts and collected war contributions until treaty agreements demarcated revised territorial boundaries. \n\n Status: Military occupation zone; Capital: None (decentralised); Official languages: Persian; Common languages: Telugu, Urdu and Deccani; Religion: Sunni Islam and Hinduism; Government: Military administrative command; Ruler title: Nizam; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1 April 1767; Disestablished: 18 March 1792; Succeeded by: Hyderabad State

name: Tahiti
description: Tahiti under British administration comprised a brief period of nominal British possession over the Polynesian island of Tahiti in the South Pacific Ocean. Claimed for King George III in June 1767 by Captain Samuel Wallis of HMS Dolphin under the name of King George the Third's Island, the territory was anchored around naval anchorages in Matavai Bay. British officers traded metal goods with indigenous ari'i chiefs but established no permanent administrative apparatus, leaving sovereign island affairs in native hands. \n\n Status: British naval possession; Capital: Papeete; Official languages: English; Common languages: Tahitian; Religion: Traditional Polynesian religion; Government: Naval protectorate; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 18 June 1767; Disestablished: 1773; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Tahiti

name: Kingdom of Mysore (Military Occupation)
description: The Kingdom of Mysore (Military Occupation) consisted of wartime territorial zones garrisoned and administered by the modernised armies of Hyder Ali and Tipu Sultan across the Carnatic, Malabar and Tamil plains. Established during the First and Second Anglo-Mysore Wars, these martial operational districts were governed by Mysorean faujdars and army commanders who mobilised agricultural resources and fortified critical routes. The military administrations persisted until formal peace accords returned the territories to civilian rule or adversary control. \n\n Status: Military occupation zone; Capital: None (decentralised); Official languages: Persian; Common languages: Kannada, Tamil and Malayalam; Religion: Sunni Islam and Hinduism; Government: Military administrative command; Head of state: Tipu Sultan; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1 October 1767; Disestablished: 11 March 1784; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Mysore

name: Kingdom of Thonburi
description: The Kingdom of Thonburi was a sovereign Siamese monarchy founded by King Taksin following the catastrophic destruction of Ayutthaya by Burmese invaders in 1767. Establishing his royal seat at Thonburi on the west bank of the Chao Phraya River, Taksin reunited the divided provinces, rebuilt the kingdom's military power and extended Siamese suzerainty over Lan Na, Cambodia and the Lao kingdoms. The dynasty fostered maritime trade with Qing China until domestic upheaval led to Taksin's deposition and the founding of the Rattanakosin Kingdom in 1782. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Thonburi; Common languages: Thai; Religion: Theravada Buddhism; Government: Absolute monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Thonburi dynasty; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 28 December 1767; Disestablished: 6 April 1782; Succeeded by: Rattanakosin Kingdom

name: Mawkmai State
label: shan states
description: Mawkmai State was a feudal Shan principality situated in the rugged southeastern Shan Hills along the Salween River drainage basin in eastern Burma. Governed from the town of Mawkmai by hereditary sawbwas, the realm was populated by Shan, Pa-O and Karen communities engaged in agriculture and teak extraction. The state remained a loyal tributary vassal to the Konbaung dynasty of Burma, providing annual tribute and troop contingents until British forces annexed the Shan States in 1886. \n\n Status: Tributary vassal state under Burma; Capital: Mawkmai; Common languages: Shan, Pa-O and Burmese; Religion: Theravada Buddhism; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Ruler title: Sawbwa; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1768; Disestablished: 1886; Succeeded by: British Burma

name: East India Company (Military Occupation)
description: The East India Company (Military Occupation) encompassed temporary martial command zones established across southern and western India during the Anglo-Mysore and Anglo-Maratha Wars. Governed directly by British military officers under martial law, these operational sectors spanned key coastal ports, fortified hill stations and contested agricultural districts in Malabar and the Carnatic. The company's armed forces secured communications, levied local taxes and maintained garrison posts until diplomatic treaties or formal annexations integrated the territories into civil presidency administration. \n\n Status: Military occupation zone; Capital: None (decentralised); Official languages: English; Common languages: English, Tamil, Telugu and Kannada; Religion: Anglicanism, Hinduism and Islam; Government: Military command under martial law; Head of state: Governor-General of India; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1 March 1768; Disestablished: 30 June 1799; Succeeded by: British East India Company

name: Emirate of Umm Al Quwain
description: The Emirate of Umm Al Quwain was an independent coastal sheikhdom situated along the Persian Gulf coast of the southeastern Arabian Peninsula. Founded in 1768 by Sheikh Majid Al Mualla of the Al Ali tribe, the realm was centred on the coastal settlement of Umm Al Quwain and the inland palm oasis of Falaj Al Mualla. The emirate prospered through maritime commerce, date cultivation and pearl fishing, maintaining its sovereignty until signing the 1820 General Maritime Treaty with Great Britain. \n\n Status: Sovereign sheikhdom; Capital: Umm Al Quwain; Common languages: Arabic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Traditional sheikhdom; Ruling dynasty: Al Mualla dynasty; Ruler title: Sheikh; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1769; Disestablished: 5 February 1820; Succeeded by: Trucial States

name: Ilam
label: nepal petty kingdoms
description: Ilam was an autonomous Himalayan hill principality situated in the eastern Mahabharata Range across the upper Mechi River watershed in modern Nepal. Inhabited by indigenous Limbu, Lepcha and Khas communities, the realm was governed by hereditary chieftains who controlled strategic mountain trade passes leading into Sikkim and Bengal. The state maintained independent agrarian governance and cultural traditions until King Prithvi Narayan Shah's Gorkha armies conquered the eastern hills and annexed Ilam into the Kingdom of Nepal in 1776. \n\n Status: Sovereign petty kingdom; Capital: Ilam; Common languages: Limbu, Nepali and Lepcha; Religion: Kirat Mundhum and Hinduism; Government: Traditional chieftaincy; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1770; Disestablished: 1776; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Nepal

name: Kingdom of Nepal
description: The Kingdom of Nepal was a sovereign Himalayan monarchy established through the military conquests of King Prithvi Narayan Shah of the Gorkha dynasty. Establishing Kathmandu as the national capital after conquering the Kathmandu Valley kingdoms, the realm rapidly expanded across the Himalayan ranges between Sikkim and Kumaon. The state developed sophisticated military institutions and defended its territorial sovereignty against the British East India Company and Qing China, enduring as an independent Hindu monarchy until the proclamation of a republic in May 2008. \n\n Status: Sovereign monarchy; Capital: Kathmandu; Official languages: Nepali; Common languages: Nepali and Newar; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Absolute monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Shah dynasty; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1770; Disestablished: 28 May 2008; Succeeded by: Federal Democratic Republic of Nepal

name: Limbuwan Kingdoms
label: nepal petty kingdoms
description: The Limbuwan Kingdoms formed a sovereign confederation of ten traditional Limbu states situated across the eastern Himalayan foothills of modern Nepal. Governed by hereditary Limbu chieftains known as subbas from their historic political centre at Bijaypur, the confederacy preserved indigenous Yakthung customs, land rights and Kirat cultural practices. The kingdoms maintained collective military defence against regional neighbours until concluding a formal peace agreement that incorporated Limbuwan into the unified Gorkha Kingdom in 1774. \n\n Status: Sovereign tribal confederation; Capital: Bijaypur; Common languages: Limbu and Nepali; Religion: Kirat Mundhum; Government: Confederal council of chieftains; Ruler title: Subba; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1770; Disestablished: 1775; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Nepal

name: Morang
label: nepal petty kingdoms
description: Morang was an autonomous principality encompassing the fertile Terai lowlands and dense subtropical forests of southeastern Nepal. Governed by indigenous Koch and Khas chieftains from their administrative seat at Biratnagar, the state commanded lucrative trade routes linking the Himalayan foothills with the northern plains of Bengal. The principality preserved its local revenue systems and political independence until the eastward expansion of the Gorkha Kingdom led to its conquest and absorption in the mid-1770s. \n\n Status: Sovereign petty kingdom; Capital: Biratnagar; Common languages: Maithili, Nepali and Bengali; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Traditional monarchy; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1770; Disestablished: 1775; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Nepal

name: Yangwarok
label: nepal petty kingdoms
description: Yangwarok was an independent Limbu hill state situated in the rugged high mountain valleys of modern Panchthar district in eastern Nepal. Governed by traditional Limbu clan leaders from the fortified settlement of Yangwarok, the realm maintained customary village councils and sustained a self-sufficient pastoral and terrace-farming economy. The state resisted Gorkha expansionist armies during the Limbuwan-Gorkha War before being conquered and integrated into the Kingdom of Nepal in 1777. \n\n Status: Sovereign petty kingdom; Capital: Yangwarok; Common languages: Limbu; Religion: Kirat Mundhum; Government: Traditional chieftaincy; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1770; Disestablished: 1777; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Nepal

name: Yashikira
description: Yashikira was a sovereign precolonial kingdom located in the Borgu borderlands between modern western Nigeria and northern Benin. Inhabited by the Bariba people, the state was ruled by a traditional monarch known as the Sinaboko from his fortified capital at Yashikira. The kingdom maintained a disciplined cavalry army that secured trade routes and repelled neighbouring Dahomean and Fulani incursions until British colonial expeditions conquered Borgu in 1900. \n\n Status: Precolonial kingdom; Capital: Yashikira; Common languages: Bariba; Religion: Traditional animism and Sunni Islam; Government: Traditional monarchy; Ruler title: Sinaboko; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1770; Disestablished: 1900; Succeeded by: Northern Nigeria Protectorate

name: Aqrabi Sheikhdom
label: southern arabia petty kingdoms
description: The Aqrabi Sheikhdom was an independent tribal principality situated along the southern Arabian littoral immediately north of the port of Aden. Ruled by hereditary sheikhs of the Aqrabi clan from their historic oasis capital at Bir Ahmad, the state controlled vital agricultural lands and overland caravan routes feeding into Aden harbour. The sheikhdom maintained its complete sovereignty through diplomatic alliances with neighbouring tribes until signing a formal British protectorate treaty in February 1890. \n\n Status: Sovereign sheikhdom; Capital: Bir Ahmad; Common languages: Arabic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Traditional sheikhdom; Ruling dynasty: Aqrabi; Ruler title: Sheikh; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1771; Disestablished: 26 February 1890; Succeeded by: Aden Protectorate

name: Bibemi
description: Bibemi was an autonomous precolonial chieftaincy situated in the northern savanna of modern Cameroon within the Benue River basin. Governed by traditional Kirdi chieftains from the settlement of Bibemi, the polity sustained an agricultural economy based on millet cultivation, cattle raising and regional trade. The chiefdom maintained its independence against surrounding ethnic groups until the early nineteenth century, when the Fulani jihad led by Modibo Adama incorporated Bibemi into the Adamawa Emirate in 1809. \n\n Status: Precolonial chieftaincy; Capital: Bibemi; Common languages: Duru languages and Fulfulde; Religion: Traditional animism; Government: Traditional chieftaincy; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1771; Disestablished: 1809; Succeeded by: Adamawa Emirate

name: Kaiama
description: Kaiama was an independent Borgu kingdom situated in the wooded savanna of modern western Kwara State in Nigeria. Founded by Bariba royalty and ruled by the Mora Tasude dynasty from the walled city of Kaiama, the kingdom maintained a formidable horse cavalry that controlled regional trade routes between Hausaland and the coast. The state vigorously defended its autonomy against the expansion of the Sokoto Caliphate until British imperial forces established the Protectorate of Northern Nigeria in 1900. \n\n Status: Precolonial kingdom; Capital: Kaiama; Common languages: Bariba and Yoruba; Religion: Traditional animism and Sunni Islam; Government: Traditional monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Mora Tasude; Ruler title: Emir of Kaiama; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1771; Disestablished: 1900; Succeeded by: Northern Nigeria Protectorate

name: Kingdom of Gumma
label: kingdoms in the gibe region
description: The Kingdom of Gumma was an independent Oromo monarchy established on the fertile highland plateau of the Gibe region in southwestern Ethiopia. Ruled by hereditary monarchs from their capital at Dembi, the kingdom was bounded by the Didessa River and flourished through intensive cultivation of wheat, barley and cotton. Gumma maintained an elite warrior caste and embraced Sunni Islam in the nineteenth century, defending its sovereignty until Emperor Menelik II conquered the realm and incorporated it into the Ethiopian Empire in 1903. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Dembi; Common languages: Oromo; Religion: Sunni Islam and traditional Oromo religion; Government: Traditional monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Gumma dynasty; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1771; Disestablished: 1903; Succeeded by: Ethiopian Empire

name: Pontianak Sultanate
description: The Pontianak Sultanate was an independent maritime Malay-Arab state established on the western coast of Borneo at the junction of the Kapuas and Landak rivers. Founded in October 1771 by Syarif Abdurrahman Alkadrie, a respected Hadhrami sayyid, the sultanate rapidly grew into a bustling trading port exporting gold, diamonds and forest products. The realm maintained complete sovereignty and established dynastic alliances with surrounding kingdoms before concluding a protective commercial treaty with the Dutch East India Company in 1780. \n\n Status: Sovereign sultanate; Capital: Pontianak; Common languages: Malay and Arabic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Islamic absolute monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Alkadrie dynasty; Ruler title: Sultan; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 23 October 1771; Disestablished: 1780; Succeeded by: Pontianak Sultanate (Dutch protectorate)

name: Namtok State
label: shan states
description: Namtok State was a tributary Shan principality situated in the Myelat division of the southern Shan States in eastern Burma. Governed from Namtok by hereditary local chieftains known as myozas, the compact territory was inhabited by Danu and Taungyo agriculturalists who cultivated rice and upland crops. The principality preserved internal autonomy while rendering annual tribute and auxiliary soldiers to the Konbaung monarchs of Burma until the British annexation of Upper Burma in 1886. \n\n Status: Tributary vassal state under Burma; Capital: Namtok; Common languages: Shan, Danu and Burmese; Religion: Theravada Buddhism; Government: Feudal lordship; Ruler title: Myoza; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1772; Disestablished: 1886; Succeeded by: British Burma

name: Crozet Islands
description: The Crozet Islands formed an isolated subantarctic archipelago in the southern Indian Ocean, discovered in January 1772 by French explorer Marc-Joseph Marion du Fresne. Named in honour of his second-in-command Jules Crozet, the wind-swept volcanic islands lacked permanent civilian inhabitants but were frequently visited by French, British and American sealing vessels. France maintained continuous sovereign claim over the territory until formally incorporating the archipelago into the French Southern and Antarctic Lands in August 1955. \n\n Status: French overseas possession; Capital: None (decentralised); Official languages: French; Religion: None (uninhabited); Government: Colonial dependency; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 24 January 1772; Disestablished: 6 August 1955; Succeeded by: French Southern and Antarctic Lands

name: Kerguelen Islands
description: The Kerguelen Islands constituted a remote, windswept volcanic archipelago in the southern Indian Ocean, discovered in February 1772 by French navigator Yves-Joseph de Kerguelen de Trémarec. Possessing a harsh subantarctic maritime climate, the rugged archipelago was never settled by an indigenous population but served as a critical base for nineteenth-century whalers, sealers and scientific expeditions. The French Crown sustained its territorial claim across successive regimes until establishing the islands as a distinct administrative district of the French Southern and Antarctic Lands in 1955. \n\n Status: French overseas possession; Capital: None (decentralised); Official languages: French; Religion: None (uninhabited); Government: Colonial dependency; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 13 February 1772; Disestablished: 6 August 1955; Succeeded by: French Southern and Antarctic Lands

name: Dirk Hartog Island
description: Dirk Hartog Island was a nominal French territorial claim on a prominent barrier island off the Gascoyne coast of Western Australia. On 28 March 1772, French navigator Louis Aleno de St Aloüarn landed on the island and formally claimed the western coast of New Holland for King Louis XV, burying an inscribed bottle and French coins. Although France established no permanent naval garrison or colonial settlement, the claim was preserved diplomatically until Great Britain annexed the entire western third of Australia in May 1829. \n\n Status: French overseas claim; Capital: None (decentralised); Official languages: French; Common languages: Malgana; Religion: None; Government: Nominal colonial possession; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 28 March 1772; Disestablished: 2 May 1829; Succeeded by: Swan River Colony

name: Kapurthala State
description: Kapurthala State was a sovereign Sikh principality established in the fertile Doaba region of the Punjab between the Beas and Sutlej rivers. Founded in 1772 by Sardar Jassa Singh Ahluwalia, the supreme military commander of the Dal Khalsa, the state was administered from the historic town of Kapurthala. The Ahluwalia rulers commanded formidable cavalry forces and governed prosperous agricultural communities before negotiating protective diplomatic agreements with the British East India Company in the early nineteenth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign princely state; Capital: Kapurthala; Common languages: Punjabi and Hindustani; Religion: Sikhism, Islam and Hinduism; Government: Princely monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Ahluwalia; Ruler title: Sardar; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1773; Disestablished: 1802; Succeeded by: Kapurthala State (British protectorate)

name: Lawa Thikana
description: Lawa Thikana was an autonomous Rajput baronial estate located in the semi-arid plains of Rajasthan near the town of Tonk. Governed by Dasawat Naruka Rajputs from their fortified estate at Lawa, the chiefship asserted territorial independence following the disintegration of Mughal imperial governance. The rulers maintained a defensive redoubt and collected land revenues while resisting neighbouring Maratha and Pindari raids until accepting British suzerainty under the Rajputana Agency in 1818. \n\n Status: Sovereign baronial estate; Capital: Lawa; Common languages: Rajasthani and Hindi; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Princely lordship; Ruling dynasty: Dasawat Naruka Rajput; Ruler title: Thakur; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1773; Disestablished: 1818; Succeeded by: Lawa Thikana (British protectorate)

name: Antongila Kingdom
description: The Antongila Kingdom was a short-lived Betsimisaraka realm established around the shores of Antongil Bay on the northeastern coast of Madagascar. Founded by Maurice Benyovszky, an adventurous Hungarian-Polish nobleman commissioned by the French Crown who was acclaimed as mpanjaka by local Malagasy chiefs, the state established regional fortifications and promoted trade with European merchants. The kingdom dissolved following Benyovszky's recall to Europe and the abandonment of the French trading settlement in July 1779. \n\n Status: Sovereign precolonial kingdom; Capital: Maroantsetra; Common languages: Malagasy and French; Religion: Traditional Malagasy beliefs; Government: Elective monarchy; Head of state: Maurice Benyovszky; Ruler title: Mpanjaka; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1 April 1773; Disestablished: 1 July 1779; Succeeded by: Merina Kingdom

name: State of Negeri Sembilan
description: The State of Negeri Sembilan was a sovereign confederation of nine traditional Minangkabau districts established in the southwestern region of the Malay Peninsula. Formed under the leadership of Raja Melewar of Pagaruyung as the first Yang di-Pertuan Besar, the realm practised matrilineal customary law and fostered thriving rice farming and tin extraction. The confederation maintained its political independence against neighbouring Johor and Bugis influences until concluding agreements that introduced a British resident in 1874. \n\n Status: Sovereign confederation of states; Capital: Seremban; Common languages: Negeri Sembilan Malay; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Elective constitutional monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Pagaruyung dynasty; Ruler title: Yang di-Pertuan Besar; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1774; Disestablished: 1874; Succeeded by: British Malaya

name: French Madagascar
description: French Madagascar comprised an overseas colonial possession encompassing trading posts and later the entire island of Madagascar off the southeastern coast of Africa. Initially founded as a trading enclave at Antongil Bay in 1774, the French presence was formalised into a unified colony in 1897 following the overthrow of the Merina monarchy. Governed by French governors-general from Antananarivo, the colony developed agricultural exports of vanilla, coffee and cloves until reorganising into an autonomous republic within the French Community in 1958. \n\n Status: Colony of France; Capital: Antananarivo; Official languages: French; Common languages: Malagasy and French; Religion: Traditional animism, Protestantism and Roman Catholicism; Government: Colonial administration; Ruler title: Governor-General; Historical era: Early modern to Modern period; Established: 1 April 1774; Disestablished: 14 October 1958; Succeeded by: Malagasy Republic

name: Rampur State
description: Rampur State was an autonomous Rohilla Afghan principality established in northern India following the settlement of the First Rohilla War in 1774. Founded by Nawab Faizullah Khan under treaty arrangements with the Nawab of Awadh and the British East India Company, the state had its capital at Rampur in the fertile plains of Rohilkhand.
