name: Turks and Caicos Islands
description: The Turks and Caicos Islands formed a British colonial dependency in the Lucayan Archipelago of the northern West Indies, formally confirmed under the Crown by the 1783 Treaty of Paris. The low-lying islands developed a thriving marine economy centred upon commercial sea-salt harvesting and maritime trade. Administered at various intervals through Bermuda, the Bahamas and Jamaica, the territory retained its distinct identity as an autonomous British dependency. \n\n Status: Crown colony; Capital: Cockburn Town; Official languages: English; Common languages: English and Turks and Caicos Creole; Religion: Christianity; Government: Parliamentary dependency; Ruler title: British monarch; Historical era: Colonial period; Established: 3 September 1783

name: Hopong State
label: shan states
description: Hopong State was a small Shan principality situated in the central division of the southern Shan States in eastern Burma. Governed by a traditional chieftain styled as a myoza, the lordship maintained local agrarian authority while acknowledging the suzerainty of the Burmese Konbaung monarchy through regular tributary missions. The territory remained subordinate to the court at Ava and Mandalay until British forces extended colonial rule across the Shan highlands in 1886. \n\n Status: Vassal state; Capital: Hopong; Common languages: Shan and Pa'O; Religion: Theravada Buddhism; Government: Feudal principality; Ruler title: Myoza; Historical region: Shan States; Historical era: Early modern period

name: Khairpur State
description: Khairpur State was an autonomous princely realm in northern Sindh established along the eastern banks of the Indus River by Mir Sohrab Khan Talpur in 1783. Following the collapse of the Kalhora dynasty, this branch of the Talpur clan ruled the territory as an independent emirate known locally as the Uttrad region. The state maintained sovereign control over its agricultural heartlands until entering defensive treaty arrangements with the British East India Company in 1839. \n\n Status: Sovereign emirate; Capital: Khairpur; Common languages: Sindhi and Balochi; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Absolute monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Talpur; Ruler title: Mir; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1783

name: Pangtara State
label: shan states
description: Pangtara State was a Shan principality located within the Myelat division of the southern Shan plateau in eastern Burma. Centred on the fertile Pindaya valley, the domain was ruled by a local hereditary chief subordinate to the Konbaung dynasty of Burma. The state fulfilled customary feudal duties and provided military levies to the Burmese court until imperial British authorities incorporated the entire region following the Third Anglo-Burmese War. \n\n Status: Vassal state; Capital: Pindaya; Common languages: Shan and Burmese; Religion: Theravada Buddhism; Government: Feudal principality; Ruler title: Myoza; Historical region: Shan States; Historical era: Early modern period

name: Sakoi State
label: shan states
description: Sakoi State was a minor Shan feudal territory situated in the rugged hill tracts of the southern Shan plateau in eastern Burma. Also recorded as Sagwe, the highland domain was administered by a local hereditary ruler who acknowledged the overarching authority of the Burmese crown. The principality preserved its customary mountain governance until the collapse of the Konbaung monarchy led to British pacification across Upper Burma in 1886. \n\n Status: Vassal state; Capital: Sakoi; Common languages: Shan; Religion: Theravada Buddhism; Government: Feudal lordship; Ruler title: Myoza; Historical region: Shan States; Historical era: Early modern period

name: Unorganized Territory
description: The Unorganised Territory comprised the residual western federal public lands of the United States that lacked formal statutory territorial organisation under an organic act of Congress. Administered directly by federal authorities and military garrisons without local legislative assemblies, these expanses accommodated indigenous populations and frontier outposts prior to formal settlement. As regional populations expanded, Congress successively subdivided and organised these vast tracts into incorporated territories and sovereign states. \n\n Status: Federal unorganised territory; Capital: None (decentralised); Official languages: English; Government: Direct federal administration; Legislature: United States Congress; Currency: United States dollar; Historical era: Early modern to Late modern period

name: Colony of Saint-Barthélemy
description: The Colony of Saint-Barthélemy was a Caribbean island dependency acquired by Sweden from France in 1784 in exchange for commercial depot rights in Gothenburg. Its capital of Gustavia was declared a free port, rapidly transforming the arid volcanic island into a prosperous entrepot for neutral maritime commerce during the Napoleonic Wars. Crown administration governed the territory directly until declining mercantile fortunes prompted Sweden to retrocede the island to France in 1878. \n\n Status: Crown colony; Capital: Gustavia; Common languages: Swedish and French; Religion: Lutheranism and Roman Catholicism; Government: Colonial administration; Head of state: King of Sweden; Currency: Swedish riksdaler; Historical era: Colonial period; Established: 1 July 1784; Disestablished: 16 March 1878

name: Sultanate of Selangor
description: The Sultanate of Selangor fell under temporary Dutch protectorate rule in August 1784 following a naval expedition launched by the Dutch East India Company against the royal capital at Kuala Selangor. Dutch forces occupied the coastal citadel of Bukit Selangor to suppress Bugis commercial influence across the Strait of Malacca. The foreign occupation was short-lived, as Sultan Ibrahim Shah rallied local forces to retake the fortress by surprise in 1786 and restore complete Malay sovereignty. \n\n Status: Dutch protectorate; Capital: Kuala Selangor; Common languages: Malay; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Sultanate under foreign military occupation; Head of state: Sultan of Selangor; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 13 August 1784; Disestablished: 29 July 1786

name: Baoni State
description: Baoni State was an autonomous Muslim princely domain established in the Betwa-Yamuna doab of northern India by Ghaziuddin Khan, a former imperial wazir connected to the Asaf Jahi dynasty of Hyderabad. Operating as a recognised jagir within the sphere of the Maratha Confederacy, the state maintained complete domestic autonomy from its seat at Kadaura. Its rulers preserved independent regional governance until concluding formal protective agreements with the British East India Company in 1807. \n\n Status: Princely state; Capital: Kadaura; Common languages: Urdu and Bundeli; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Princely jagir; Ruling dynasty: Asaf Jahi cadet branch; Ruler title: Nawab; Historical region: Bundelkhand; Established: 1784

name: Kenu
description: Kenu was a traditional agrarian principality situated in the Borgu borderlands between modern Benin and western Nigeria. Centred upon its fortified settlement, the polity preserved sovereign local governance and regulated regional trade routes connecting the Niger valley with the Yoruba hinterland. The chieftaincy maintained complete independence until Anglo-French imperial boundary commissions partitioned the Borgu region at the close of the nineteenth century. \n\n Status: Traditional chieftaincy; Capital: Kenu; Common languages: Bariba; Religion: Traditional African religion and Islam; Government: Tribal monarchy; Ruler title: Chief; Historical region: Borgu; Historical era: Pre-colonial Africa; Disestablished: 1900

name: Kingdom of Sigave
description: The Kingdom of Sigave was a traditional Polynesian monarchy occupying the western half of Futuna Island in the South Pacific Ocean. Governed by a paramount king known as the Keletaona alongside a council of hereditary clan chiefs, the realm maintained customary communal landholdings and maritime traditions. The kingdom retained uninterrupted sovereignty until November 1887, when its leadership accepted a formal protectorate treaty with the French Republic. \n\n Status: Traditional monarchy; Capital: Leava; Common languages: Futunan; Religion: Traditional Polynesian religion and Roman Catholicism; Government: Traditional chieftaincy; Ruler title: Keletaona; Historical region: Polynesia; Historical era: Pre-colonial Pacific; Disestablished: 29 November 1887

name: Chhatarpur State
description: Chhatarpur State was an autonomous princely realm founded in 1785 by Kunwar Sone Shah Ponwar in the Bundelkhand region of central India. Taking advantage of the decline of local Bundela power, the Ponwar dynasty established sovereign control over its capital and surrounding agricultural territories. The state maintained self-governing authority until the early nineteenth century, when it entered into subsidiary alliance treaties under British paramountcy. \n\n Status: Princely state; Capital: Chhatarpur; Common languages: Bundeli and Hindi; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Princely monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Ponwar Rajput; Ruler title: Raja; Historical region: Bundelkhand; Established: 1785

name: Emirate of Bukhara
description: The Emirate of Bukhara was an absolute Islamic monarchy established in Transoxiana in 1785 following the rise of the Manghit dynasty under Shah Murad. Centred upon the historic oasis cities of Bukhara and Samarkand along the Zarafshan River, the state functioned as a major diplomatic and religious power in Central Asia. The emirate retained full sovereign autonomy until Russian imperial armies invaded the region and imposed a protectorate regime in 1868. \n\n Status: Sovereign emirate; Capital: Bukhara; Common languages: Persian and Chagatai Turkic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Absolute monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Manghit; Ruler title: Emir; Historical era: Early modern to Late modern period; Established: 1785

name: Kotokoli
description: Kotokoli was an autonomous confederation of chiefdoms founded by the Tem people in the central plateau of modern Togo. Governed by a supreme paramount monarch titled the Wuro from his seat at Sokodé, the polity controlled prosperous north-south caravan tracks linking the Sahel with the Atlantic coast. The realm defended its independence and traditional customs until German colonial forces occupied the interior and established the Togoland protectorate in 1896. \n\n Status: Traditional confederation; Capital: Sokodé; Common languages: Tem; Religion: Islam and Traditional African religion; Government: Paramount chieftaincy; Ruler title: Wuro; Historical region: West Africa; Historical era: Pre-colonial Africa; Disestablished: 1896

name: Kpangalam
description: Kpangalam was a traditional Gur-speaking chieftaincy domain situated near Sokodé in the central tablelands of modern Togo. Closely aligned with the broader Kotokoli political alliance, the community governed its agrarian settlements through customary councils of elders and local warrior leaders. The polity preserved its autonomy and commercial ties with surrounding regional markets until the imposition of imperial German colonial administration in 1896. \n\n Status: Traditional chieftaincy; Capital: Kpangalam; Common languages: Tem; Religion: Traditional African religion and Islam; Government: Chieftaincy; Ruler title: Chief; Historical region: West Africa; Historical era: Pre-colonial Africa; Disestablished: 1896

name: Princely County of Scheer
label: holy roman empire
description: The Princely County of Scheer was an immediate imperial territory of the Holy Roman Empire located along the upper Danube River in Swabia. Possessed by the princely House of Thurn und Taxis from 1786, the domain exercised territorial sovereignty and held voting rights within the imperial diet. The county retained its self-governing status until the reorganisation of south German lands during the Napoleonic mediatisation annexed its territory to neighbouring Württemberg and Hohenzollern. \n\n Status: Imperial county; Capital: Scheer; Official languages: German; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Thurn und Taxis; Historical region: Swabia; Historical era: Early modern period; Disestablished: 1807

name: Principality of Hà Tiên
description: The Principality of Hà Tiên was an autonomous coastal domain established on the Gulf of Thailand by the Chinese Mạc dynasty. Situated at the junction of Vietnamese and Cambodian cultural zones, the thriving maritime entrepot maintained strategic neutrality by acknowledging dual vassalage to both the Siamese Rattanakosin monarchy and the Vietnamese imperial court. The principality preserved its hereditary leadership and Chinese administrative heritage until its complete integration into the Vietnamese provincial system. \n\n Status: Dual protectorate; Capital: Hà Tiên; Common languages: Vietnamese, Cantonese and Southern Min; Religion: Mahayana Buddhism and Confucianism; Government: Principality; Ruling dynasty: Mạc; Ruler title: Governor; Historical era: Early modern period

name: Principality of Wied-Runkel
label: holy roman empire
description: The Principality of Wied-Runkel was an immediate sovereign principality of the Holy Roman Empire situated in the Westerwald and Lahn regions of western Germany. Formed through the historic territorial partitions of the House of Wied, the realm was elevated to princely dignity and ruled from its administrative seat at Dierdorf. The principality maintained autonomous feudal governance until French Revolutionary military campaigns and nineteenth-century mediatisation absorbed its lands into Nassau. \n\n Status: Principality of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Dierdorf; Official languages: German; Religion: Lutheranism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Wied; Ruler title: Prince; Historical era: Early modern period; Disestablished: 1806

name: United Indian Nations
description: The United Indian Nations, historically designated the Northwestern Confederacy, was a pan-tribal alliance formed by indigenous nations of the Great Lakes and Ohio River basin to halt American territorial encroachment. Convening at general confederate councils around Kekionga, the alliance united Miami, Shawnee, Wyandot and Delaware warriors to defend Native lands following the 1783 Treaty of Paris. The confederacy achieved major military successes during the Northwest Indian War before internal fractures and the 1794 Battle of Fallen Timbers compelled peace negotiations. \n\n Status: Pan-tribal confederacy; Capital: None (decentralised); Common languages: Miami, Shawnee, Delaware and Wyandot; Religion: Traditional indigenous beliefs; Government: Confederated council of chiefs; Historical region: Old Northwest; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1786; Disestablished: 1795

name: Prince of Wales Island
description: Prince of Wales Island was a British crown colony established on Penang Island off the north-western coast of Peninsular Malaysia following its cession by the Sultan of Kedah in 1786. Developed by Captain Francis Light as an East India Company free port, the settlement at George Town attracted diverse communities of Chinese, Malay and Indian merchants. The colony flourished as a pivotal maritime trading post before being merged into the unified administration of the Straits Settlements in 1826. \n\n Status: Crown colony; Capital: George Town; Official languages: English; Common languages: English, Malay, Hokkien and Tamil; Government: Colonial governorship; Head of state: British monarch; Historical era: Colonial period; Established: 11 August 1786; Succeeded by: Straits Settlements

name: Akwa Akpa
description: Akwa Akpa was an autonomous Efik city-state situated along the lower Calabar River estuary near the Bight of Biafra in south-eastern Nigeria. Known to European traders as Duke Town or Old Calabar, the kingdom was governed by prominent merchant houses coordinated through the prestigious Ekpe secret society. The city-state served as an influential commercial hub for palm oil exports until British authorities incorporated the domain into the Oil Rivers Protectorate in 1891. \n\n Status: Sovereign city-state; Capital: Calabar; Common languages: Efik; Religion: Traditional religion and Christianity; Government: Monarchy with Ekpe council; Ruler title: Obong; Historical region: Bight of Biafra; Established: 1787; Disestablished: 1891

name: Swedish West India Company
description: The Swedish West India Company was a chartered commercial corporation empowered by King Gustav III to administer the Caribbean island colony of Saint-Barthélemy. Operating from the free port of Gustavia, the company exercised civil governance, collected maritime customs and managed transatlantic trading monopolies on behalf of private investors and the Swedish Crown. Direct royal governance replaced company rule in 1805 following administrative reorganisation and shifting commercial priorities in the West Indies. \n\n Status: Chartered company rule; Capital: Gustavia; Common languages: Swedish and French; Government: Commercial monopoly administration; Historical era: Colonial period; Established: 1786; Disestablished: 1805; Preceded by: Colony of Saint-Barthélemy; Succeeded by: Colony of Saint-Barthélemy

name: Colony of New South Wales
label: british colonies in australia
description: The Colony of New South Wales was a British Crown colony established on the eastern coast of Australia following the arrival of the First Fleet under Governor Arthur Phillip in 1788. Initially founded as a penal settlement encompassing vast areas of the continent, the colony expanded through agricultural settlement, pastoral enterprise and maritime commerce. Responsible parliamentary self-government was instituted in 1856, culminating in the colony becoming a founding state of the Commonwealth of Australia in 1901. \n\n Status: Crown colony; Capital: Sydney; Official languages: English; Religion: Christianity; Government: Constitutional colonial administration; Ruler title: British monarch; Legislature: Parliament of New South Wales; Established: 25 April 1787; Disestablished: 1 January 1901

name: Territory Northwest of the River Ohio
description: The Territory Northwest of the River Ohio, commonly termed the Northwest Territory, was an organised incorporated territory of the United States created by the Congress of the Confederation under the 1787 Northwest Ordinance. Encompassing the expansive region between the Ohio River, the Great Lakes and the Mississippi River, the territory established seminal legal precedents by prohibiting slavery and guaranteeing civil liberties. The entity was dissolved in 1803 when its south-eastern district entered the Union as the State of Ohio. \n\n Status: Organised incorporated territory; Capital: Chillicothe; Official languages: English; Government: Territorial administration; Ruler title: Governor; Legislature: Territorial Assembly; Preceded by: Province of Quebec; Succeeded by: Ohio and Indiana Territory; Established: 13 July 1787; Disestablished: 1 March 1803

name: Colony and Protectorate of Sierra Leone
description: The Colony and Protectorate of Sierra Leone was a British colonial possession established on the coast of West Africa as a settlement for destitute freed slaves and loyalist settlers. Originally administered by philanthropic organisations and the Sierra Leone Company, the territory became a formal Crown colony in 1808 and later extended protectorate administration over the inland peoples. Freetown functioned as the primary British naval base for anti-slavery patrols until Sierra Leone achieved national independence in 1961. \n\n Status: Crown colony and protectorate; Capital: Freetown; Official languages: English; Common languages: English and Krio; Religion: Christianity and Islam; Government: Colonial governorship; Ruler title: British monarch; Established: 1788; Disestablished: 27 April 1961

name: Côn Sơn Island
description: Côn Sơn Island was an insular possession off the southern coast of Vietnam ceded to the Kingdom of France under the 1787 Treaty of Versailles negotiated by Pigneau de Béhaine. Although direct colonial exploitation developed slowly, French naval and colonial authorities eventually developed the archipelago into a heavily fortified penal settlement and administrative station. The island remained under French colonial jurisdiction in Indochina until the Geneva Accords concluded the Indochina War in 1954. \n\n Status: French colonial dependency; Capital: None (decentralised); Common languages: French and Vietnamese; Religion: Roman Catholicism and Buddhism; Government: Colonial military administration; Historical region: Indochina; Established: 1788; Disestablished: 21 July 1954

name: Pashalik of Yanina
description: The Pashalik of Yanina was an autonomous province of the Ottoman Empire centred in Epirus and ruled by the ruthless despot Ali Pasha of Tepelena. While nominally subordinate to the Sultan in Constantinople, Ali Pasha wielded quasi-independent power across mainland Greece, Albania and Thessaly through extensive military forces and autonomous foreign diplomacy. His assertive defiance of central imperial authority eventually prompted Sultan Mahmud II to order imperial armies to besiege and destroy his regime in 1822. \n\n Status: Autonomous Ottoman eyalet; Capital: Yanina; Common languages: Greek, Albanian and Ottoman Turkish; Religion: Islam and Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Hereditary governorship; Ruler title: Pasha; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1787; Disestablished: 1 February 1822

name: Banda State
description: Banda State was an autonomous Maratha princely domain established in the Bundelkhand region of northern India during late eighteenth-century military campaigns. Founded under Nawab Ali Bahadur I, a grandson of Peshwa Baji Rao I, the realm commanded agricultural territories around the central fortress city of Banda. The state preserved local princely governance amidst shifting regional alliances until later political restructuring integrated the territory into British Bundelkhand Agency oversight. \n\n Status: Princely state; Capital: Banda; Common languages: Bundeli and Urdu; Religion: Islam and Hinduism; Government: Princely monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Nawab of Banda; Ruler title: Nawab; Historical region: Bundelkhand; Established: 1789

name: Kingdom of Lo
label: nepal petty kingdoms
description: The Kingdom of Lo was a remote Buddhist mountain realm situated in the Upper Mustang region of the northern Himalayas. In 1789 the kingdom accepted tributary vassalage under the expanding Gorkha monarchy of Nepal while retaining its hereditary raja, fortified capital at Lo Manthang and Tibetan cultural traditions. The kingdom continued to operate with autonomous internal feudal institutions under Nepalese suzerainty until the formal abolition of the monarchy in 2008. \n\n Status: Vassal kingdom; Capital: Lo Manthang; Common languages: Tibetic languages and Nepali; Religion: Tibetan Buddhism; Government: Traditional monarchy; Ruler title: Raja; Historical region: Mustang; Established: 1380; Disestablished: 7 October 2008

name: Kingdom of Nepal (Military Occupation)
description: The Kingdom of Nepal operated military occupation administrations across conquered peripheral territories during its late eighteenth-century and nineteenth-century Himalayan expansion. Commanded directly by Gorkha generals and mobile military garrisons, these occupied zones in the Kumaon, Garhwal and Tibetan border regions enforced martial order and secured strategic mountain frontiers. The transitional martial regimes persisted until border treaties or civil administrative reorganisations formally integrated or retroceded the affected lands. \n\n Status: Military occupation zone; Administrative seat: Mobile court; Common languages: Nepali; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Military administration; Head of state: King of Nepal; Historical era: Early modern to Late modern period

name: Đại Việt
description: Đại Việt was reunited under the rule of the Tây Sơn dynasty following Emperor Quang Trung's decisive defeat of an invading Qing imperial army in early 1789. Governed from the imperial citadel of Phú Xuân, the state implemented military reforms, fostered commercial development and promoted vernacular Chữ Nôm as the administrative script. The dynasty struggled to consolidate succession after the emperor's untimely death, ultimately succumbing to the forces of Nguyễn Ánh in 1802. \n\n Status: Sovereign empire; Capital: Phú Xuân; Official languages: Vietnamese; Common languages: Vietnamese; Religion: Vietnamese folk religion, Buddhism and Taoism; Government: Absolute monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Tây Sơn; Ruler title: Emperor; Established: 3 February 1789; Disestablished: 1 June 1802

name: United Belgian States
description: The United Belgian States was a short-lived confederal republic established across the Southern Netherlands following the outbreak of the Brabant Revolution against Habsburg Emperor Joseph II. Representatives from the liberated provinces convened a Sovereign Congress in Brussels, proclaiming national independence and coordinating mutual military defence. Deep ideological divisions between conservative Statists and progressive Vonckists weakened the infant republic, allowing imperial Austrian forces to reoccupy the territory in December 1790. \n\n Status: Confederal republic; Capital: Brussels; Common languages: Dutch and French; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Confederal republic; Legislature: Sovereign Congress; Historical era: Age of Revolution; Established: 11 January 1790; Disestablished: 2 December 1790

name: Territory South of the River Ohio
description: The Territory South of the River Ohio, commonly designated the Southwest Territory, was an organised incorporated territory created by the United States Congress from lands ceded by North Carolina. Governed by William Blount from Knoxville, the administration managed frontier expansion, constructed regional roads and negotiated treaties with neighbouring Cherokee and Creek nations. The territory fulfilled its statutory mandate in 1796 when its population met requirements for admission to the Union as the State of Tennessee. \n\n Status: Organised incorporated territory; Capital: Knoxville; Official languages: English; Government: Territorial administration; Ruler title: Governor; Legislature: Territorial Assembly; Preceded by: North Carolina; Succeeded by: Tennessee; Established: 26 May 1790; Disestablished: 1 June 1796

name: Kingdom of Coorg
description: The Kingdom of Coorg was a highland monarchy situated along the summit ridge of the Western Ghats in southern India, ruled by the Haleri dynasty. Following the eviction of occupying Mysore forces during the Third Anglo-Mysore War, Raja Doddavira Rajendra entered into a formal protectorate treaty with the British East India Company in October 1790. The kingdom maintained domestic autonomy and supported British military operations until political strife led to direct British annexation in 1834. \n\n Status: British protectorate; Capital: Madikeri; Common languages: Kodava and Kannada; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Princely monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Haleri; Ruler title: Maharaja; Historical region: Kodagu; Disestablished: 6 April 1834

name: Anglo-Spanish Condominium
description: The Anglo-Spanish Condominium was a joint maritime and colonial regime established along the Pacific Northwest coast of North America under the Nootka Sound Conventions of 1790. Negotiated to resolve a major diplomatic crisis between Great Britain and Spain, the accord provided for shared commercial access, navigation rights and unfortified trading posts without establishing exclusive territorial sovereignty. The joint arrangement governed coastal interaction until Spain formally relinquished all claims north of the 42nd parallel in 1819. \n\n Status: Colonial condominium; Capital: None (decentralised); Common languages: English, Spanish and Nuu-chah-nulth; Government: Shared naval and mercantile administration; Historical region: Pacific Northwest; Established: 28 October 1790; Disestablished: 22 February 1819

name: Changbhakar State
description: Changbhakar State was an autonomous princely realm situated in the rugged hill tracts of modern Chhattisgarh in central India. Established around 1790 by Rajput chieftains of the Chauhan clan, the small principality exercised traditional agrarian rule over its rural villages and forest tracts. The domain preserved self-governing authority until concluding protective treaties under the British Chhattisgarh States Agency in 1822. \n\n Status: Princely state; Capital: Bharatpur; Common languages: Chhattisgarhi and Bagheli; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Princely monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Chauhan Rajput; Ruler title: Raja; Historical region: Chhattisgarh; Established: 1790; Disestablished: 1948

name: Kingdom of Hawaii
description: The Kingdom of Hawaii was a sovereign Polynesian archipelagic monarchy founded by Kamehameha I, who unified the Hawaiian Islands through military conquest and diplomacy. Gaining formal international recognition from major European powers and the United States, the kingdom adopted constitutional government and modern legal codes. The monarchy guided the nation through intense geopolitical pressures until American-backed commercial interests overthrew Queen Liliʻuokalani in 1893. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Honolulu; Common languages: Hawaiian and English; Religion: Hawaiian religion and Protestantism; Government: Constitutional monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Kamehameha; Ruler title: Monarch; Established: 1795; Disestablished: 17 January 1893

name: Kingdom of Jimma
label: kingdoms in the gibe region
description: The Kingdom of Jimma was an autonomous Oromo Muslim state that emerged in the fertile Gibe basin of south-western Ethiopia during the late eighteenth century. Under monarchs styled as moti, the realm commanded formidable regional military forces and controlled vital trade routes in coffee and agrarian produce. The state retained full sovereign independence until King Abba Jifar II negotiated autonomous vassal status within the expanding Ethiopian Empire in 1890. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Jiren; Common languages: Oromo; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Absolute monarchy; Ruler title: Moti; Historical region: Gibe; Established: 1737; Disestablished: 1932

name: Kingdom of Limmu-Ennarea
label: kingdoms in the gibe region
description: The Kingdom of Limmu-Ennarea was a prosperous Oromo commercial realm situated in the forested highlands of the Gibe region in south-western Ethiopia. Centred upon its bustling marketplace at Saqa, the kingdom became a pre-eminent hub for long-distance caravan trade connecting the Ethiopian interior with coastal ports. Its monarchs converted to Islam in the early nineteenth century and preserved sovereign rule until rival regional powers eclipsed the state. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Saqa; Common languages: Oromo; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical region: Gibe; Preceded by: Ennarea; Established: 1801; Disestablished: 1891

name: Kingdom of Tahiti
description: The Kingdom of Tahiti was a Polynesian island monarchy established by paramount chief Pōmare I, who unified Tahiti and neighbouring archipelagos with the assistance of British traders and firearms. Adopting Christianity and codified statutory laws under Pōmare II, the kingdom maintained independent maritime governance and engaged extensively in Pacific commerce. The state preserved its sovereign status until yielding to French naval pressure and accepting a formal protectorate in 1842. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Papeete; Common languages: Tahitian and English; Religion: Traditional Tahitian religion and Protestantism; Government: Absolute monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Pōmare; Ruler title: Monarch; Established: 1791; Disestablished: 29 June 1880

name: Kwande
description: Kwande was a traditional Bariba principality situated in the northern Borgu borderlands between modern Benin and western Nigeria. Governed by hereditary chieftains upholding ancient warrior traditions, the polity preserved sovereign local administration and defended its agricultural settlements against neighbouring regional incursions. The chieftaincy maintained uninterrupted self-rule until Anglo-French imperial boundary expeditions partitioned the Borgu territories in 1895. \n\n Status: Traditional chieftaincy; Capital: Kwande; Common languages: Bariba; Religion: Traditional African religion and Islam; Government: Traditional monarchy; Ruler title: Chief; Historical region: Borgu; Historical era: Pre-colonial Africa; Disestablished: 1895

name: Obioko
description: Obioko was an autonomous Efik community and settlement domain situated in the Cross River estuary adjacent to Calabar in south-eastern Nigeria. Governed through the traditional authority of local merchant elders and the judicial council of the Ekpe society, the polity regulated riverine trade and communal lands. The domain maintained internal self-governance until British colonial authorities annexed the surrounding oil-producing regions in 1891. \n\n Status: Traditional city-state settlement; Capital: Creek Town; Common languages: Efik; Religion: Traditional African religion and Christianity; Government: Chieftaincy with Ekpe council; Ruler title: Chief; Historical region: Bight of Biafra; Established: 1791; Disestablished: 1891

name: Sachin State
description: Sachin State was an autonomous princely realm in western India established in 1791 by Sidi Abdul Karim Mohammad Yakut Khan I, descended from the Habshi dynasty of Janjira. Located within the fertile Surat coastal plain of Gujarat, the principality exercised full internal sovereignty over its rural territories. The realm maintained independent governance until concluding protective subsidiary agreements with the British East India Company in 1802. \n\n Status: Princely state; Capital: Sachin; Common languages: Gujarati and Urdu; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Princely monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Sidi; Ruler title: Nawab; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 6 June 1791; Disestablished: 1948

name: Slave Rebels
description: The Slave Rebels constituted the revolutionary insurgent armies formed by enslaved Black labourers across northern Saint-Domingue following the historic August 1791 rebellion. Commanded by leaders such as Dutty Boukman and later Toussaint Louverture, the insurgents defeated French colonial garrisons and foreign intervention forces across the island. Their resilient struggle overthrew the plantation slave regime, culminating in the establishment of the independent nation of Haiti in 1804. \n\n Status: Revolutionary insurgent state; Capital: None (decentralised); Common languages: Haitian Creole and French; Religion: Haitian Vodou and Catholicism; Government: Revolutionary military council; Historical era: Age of Revolution; Established: 24 August 1791; Succeeded by: Empire of Haiti

name: Bonaire
description: Bonaire was a Dutch Caribbean island colony in the Leeward Antilles administered under the authority of the Netherlands following the dissolution of the Dutch West India Company. Centred at the administrative port of Kralendijk, the island maintained an economy predominantly focused upon state-managed salt evaporation pans and maritime grazing. The colony preserved its distinct colonial administration until constitutional reforms integrated it into the Netherlands Antilles in 1954. \n\n Status: Dutch colony; Administrative seat: Kralendijk; Official languages: Dutch; Common languages: Papiamento and Dutch; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Colonial administration; Historical region: Caribbean; Established: 16 March 1792; Disestablished: 15 December 1954

name: Colony of Curaçao and Dependencies
description: The Colony of Curaçao and Dependencies was a Dutch colonial territory encompassing Curaçao alongside neighbouring islands including Aruba and Bonaire in the southern Caribbean Sea. Governed from the fortified mercantile hub of Willemstad, the colony operated as a vital transhipment centre for regional commerce across the Americas.
